concepts: Magnitude of a vector, dot product and sum of vectors
questions.question: If $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c$ are unit vectors satisfying $|\vec a-\vec b|^2+|\vec b-\vec c|^2+|\vec c-\vec a|^2=9$, then $|2\vec a+5\vec b+5\vec c|$ is:
questions.key_idea: The given sum equals $9-|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2$, so the value $9$ forces $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$.
solution: For unit vectors, $|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2-2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$, and similarly for the other two pairs. Adding the three: $6-2\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b=9$.
Hence $\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec b\cdot\vec c+\vec c\cdot\vec a=-\frac32$ ...(1)
Now $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2\ge0$, that is, $\sum\vec a^2+2\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b\ge0$, i.e. $3+2\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b\ge0$.
So $\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b\ge-\frac32$, and (1) says the minimum value is attained (equality).
Equality holds only when $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|=0$, so $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$.
Therefore $5\vec b+5\vec c=-5\vec a$.
Then $2\vec a+5\vec b+5\vec c=2\vec a-5\vec a=-3\vec a$.
$|2\vec a+5\vec b+5\vec c|=3|\vec a|=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the identity $\sum|\vec a-\vec b|^2=3\sum|\vec a|^2-|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2$, which gives $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|$ in one line.
solution: Expand each term: $|\vec a-\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec b$, and add the three cyclic terms.
Each vector appears in two of the terms, so $\sum|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2\sum|\vec a|^2-2\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b$.
Also $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=\sum|\vec a|^2+2\sum\vec a\cdot\vec b$. Adding these two relations gives $\sum|\vec a-\vec b|^2+|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=3\sum|\vec a|^2$.
With unit vectors the right side is $3\cdot3=9$, and the sum of squared differences is $9$, so $|\vec a+\vec b+\vec c|^2=0$.
Hence $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$ (geometrically the three unit vectors are $120^\circ$ apart), so $2\vec a+5\vec b+5\vec c=-3\vec a$.
Its magnitude is $3$.

useful_results: For any vectors, $\sum_{i<j}|\vec a_i-\vec a_j|^2=n\sum|\vec a_i|^2-\left|\sum\vec a_i\right|^2$; for three unit vectors the sum of squared sides is at most $9$, with equality iff $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$.
Three unit vectors with zero sum are coplanar, pairwise at $120^\circ$, and satisfy $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec b\cdot\vec c=\vec c\cdot\vec a=-\frac12$.
If $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec 0$ then any combination $p\vec a+q\vec b+r\vec c$ reduces to a combination of two of them, e.g. $2\vec a+5\vec b+5\vec c=-3\vec a$.
Rule: a given value that equals the extreme (maximum or minimum) of a non-negative expression usually forces the equality case.

concepts: Vector product, parallel vectors and dot product
questions.question: If $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are vectors such that $|\vec a+\vec b|=\sqrt{29}$ and $\vec a\times(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)=(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)\times\vec b$, then a possible value of $(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot(-7\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec u=\vec u\times\vec b$ rearranges to $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec u=\vec 0$, so $\vec a+\vec b$ is parallel to $\vec u$.
solution: Let $\vec u=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$. The condition is $\vec a\times\vec u=\vec u\times\vec b=-\vec b\times\vec u$.
So $\vec a\times\vec u+\vec b\times\vec u=\vec 0$, i.e. $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec u=\vec 0$.
Hence $\vec a+\vec b=\lambda\vec u=\lambda(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)$ for some scalar $\lambda$.
$|\vec a+\vec b|=\sqrt{29}$ and $|\vec u|=\sqrt{4+9+16}=\sqrt{29}$, so $|\lambda|=1$.
Taking $\lambda=1$: $\vec a+\vec b=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$.
$(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot(-7\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)=-14+6+12=4$, which is option (C) (for $\lambda=-1$ the value would be $-4$, not in the options).

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat the cross-product condition as equality in Cauchy-Schwarz: $|\vec s\times\vec u|=0$ forces $\vec s\cdot\vec u=\pm|\vec s||\vec u|$.
solution: Let $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec u=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$; the condition reduces to $\vec s\times\vec u=\vec 0$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec s\times\vec u|^2=|\vec s|^2|\vec u|^2-(\vec s\cdot\vec u)^2=0$, so $(\vec s\cdot\vec u)^2=29\cdot29$ and $\vec s\cdot\vec u=\pm29$.
Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz means $\vec s=\frac{\vec s\cdot\vec u}{|\vec u|^2}\vec u=\pm\vec u$.
Then $\vec s\cdot(-7\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k)=\pm\,\vec u\cdot(-7,2,3)=\pm(-14+6+12)=\pm4$.
Only $+4$ appears among the options, so the answer is (C) 4.

useful_results: $\vec x\times\vec u=\vec 0$ with $\vec u\ne\vec 0$ holds iff $\vec x=\lambda\vec u$; then $|\vec x|=|\lambda||\vec u|$ fixes $\lambda$ up to sign.

$\vec a\times\vec u=\vec u\times\vec b$ is equivalent to $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec u=\vec 0$ (cross product is anti-commutative); similarly $\vec a\times\vec u=-\vec u\times\vec b$ would give $(\vec a-\vec b)\times\vec u=\vec 0$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec x\times\vec y|^2=|\vec x|^2|\vec y|^2-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)^2$.
A condition with a magnitude gives two directions (both signs of $\lambda$); always test both against the options.

concepts: Intersection of a line and a plane, foot of the perpendicular in 3D
questions.question: The point $P$ is the intersection of the straight line joining the points $Q(2,3,5)$ and $R(1,-1,4)$ with the plane $5x-4y-z=1$. If $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $T(2,1,4)$ to $QR$, then the length of the line segment $PS$ is:
questions.key_idea: $TQ=TR$, so the foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to $QR$ is the midpoint of $QR$.
solution: The line $QR$ has direction $(1,4,1)$: $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-3}{4}=\frac{z-5}{1}=\lambda$, so a general point is $(\lambda+2,\,4\lambda+3,\,\lambda+5)$.
Put it in the plane: $5(\lambda+2)-4(4\lambda+3)-(\lambda+5)=1$, i.e. $5\lambda+10-16\lambda-12-\lambda-5=1$.
This gives $-12\lambda-7=1$, so $\lambda=-\frac23$.
Therefore $P=\left(\frac43,\frac13,\frac{13}{3}\right)$.
$TQ=\sqrt{0+4+1}=\sqrt5$ and $TR=\sqrt{1+4+0}=\sqrt5$, so $TQ=TR$.
In an isosceles triangle the foot of the perpendicular from the apex falls on the midpoint of the base, so $S$ is the midpoint of $QR$: $S=\left(\frac32,1,\frac92\right)$.
$PS=\sqrt{\left(\frac43-\frac32\right)^2+\left(\frac13-1\right)^2+\left(\frac{13}{3}-\frac92\right)^2}=\sqrt{\frac1{36}+\frac{16}{36}+\frac1{36}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ units.

alternate_solutions.idea: Both $P$ and $S$ lie on $QR$, so $PS=|\Delta\lambda|\cdot|\text{direction vector}|$ using the line's parameter.
solution: Parametrise $QR$ as $Q+\mu(R-Q)$, with $R-Q=(-1,-4,-1)$, so $|R-Q|=\sqrt{18}$ and $\mu=0$ at $Q$, $\mu=1$ at $R$.
$S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $T$: $\mu_S=\frac{(T-Q)\cdot(R-Q)}{|R-Q|^2}=\frac{(0,-2,-1)\cdot(-1,-4,-1)}{18}=\frac{9}{18}=\frac12$.
Both points are on the same line, so $PS=|\mu_P-\mu_S|\,|R-Q|=\frac16\sqrt{18}$.
Hence $PS=\frac{3\sqrt2}{6}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $T$ to the line $Q+\mu\vec d$ is at $\mu=\frac{(T-Q)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$; if $TQ=TR$ it is simply the midpoint of $QR$.
For two points on one line with parameters $\mu_1,\mu_2$, the distance is $|\mu_1-\mu_2|\,|\vec d|$, with no need for coordinates.
Line meets plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=k$ where $\mu=\frac{k-\vec n\cdot Q}{\vec n\cdot\vec d}$ (valid if $\vec n\cdot\vec d\ne0$; otherwise the line is parallel to the plane).
Here, with $\vec d=R-Q=(-1,-4,-1)$: $\vec n\cdot\vec d=12$ and $\vec n\cdot Q=-7$, so $\mu=\frac{1+7}{12}=\frac23$, the point $P$.

concepts: Family of planes through the line of intersection of two planes and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: The equation of a plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes $x+2y+3z=2$ and $x-y+z=3$ and at a distance $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ from the point $(3,1,-1)$ is:
questions.key_idea: A plane through the line is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; in the distance condition the $\lambda^2$ terms cancel and leave a linear equation in $\lambda$.
solution: Let the plane be $(x+2y+3z-2)+\lambda(x-y+z-3)=0$.
Its distance from $(3,1,-1)$ is $\frac2{\sqrt3}$: $\frac{|(3+2-3-2)+\lambda(3-1-1-3)|}{\sqrt{(1+\lambda)^2+(2-\lambda)^2+(3+\lambda)^2}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.
The numerator is $|-2\lambda|$, so $\lambda^2=\frac{(1+\lambda)^2+(2-\lambda)^2+(3+\lambda)^2}{3}$ after squaring.
$3\lambda^2=3\lambda^2+2\lambda-4\lambda+6\lambda+14$, i.e. $3\lambda^2=3\lambda^2+4\lambda+14$.
The $\lambda^2$ terms cancel, leaving $4\lambda=-14$, so $\lambda=-\frac72$.
The plane is $(x+2y+3z-2)-\frac72(x-y+z-3)=0$.
Multiplying by $-2$: $5x-11y+z=17$, option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Pick two points on the line of intersection and test which option plane contains both and is at distance $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.
solution: Points on the line: $(1,-1,1)$ (check: $1-2+3=2$, $1+1+1=3$) and $\left(\frac83,-\frac13,0\right)$ (check: $\frac83-\frac23=2$, $\frac83+\frac13=3$).
A required plane must contain both points. Test (A): $5(1)-11(-1)+1=17$ and $5\cdot\frac83-11\cdot\left(-\frac13\right)+0=\frac{51}{3}=17$. Both hold.

At $(1,-1,1)$: (B) gives $\sqrt2x+y=\sqrt2-1
e3\sqrt2-1$; (C) gives $x+y+z=1
e\sqrt3$; (D) gives $x-\sqrt2y=1+\sqrt2
e1-\sqrt2$. So (B), (C), (D) do not contain the line.
So (A) satisfies both conditions.

useful_results: Every plane through the line $P_1=0,\ P_2=0$ is $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (all planes except $P_2=0$ itself, which is the $\lambda\to\infty$ case) - check $P_2$ separately.
Here $P_2: x-y+z=3$ is also at distance $\frac{|3-1-1-3|}{\sqrt3}=\frac2{\sqrt3}$ from $(3,1,-1)$, so it is a second valid plane that the $\lambda$-form misses (it is not in the options).
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
When a quadratic in $\lambda$ collapses to a linear equation it signals the excluded plane is a solution; count solutions as (roots) + (the plane $P_2$ if it satisfies the condition).

concepts: Coplanarity of two lines and equation of the plane containing them
questions.question: If the straight lines $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{k}=\frac{z}{2}$ and $\frac{x+1}{5}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z}{k}$ are coplanar, then the plane(s) containing these two lines is(are):
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity gives $2(k^2-4)=0$, so $k=\pm2$; each $k$ gives its own plane with normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.
solution: The lines pass through $A(1,-1,0)$ and $B(-1,-1,0)$ with direction ratios $(2,k,2)$ and $(5,2,k)$.
Coplanarity: $\left|\begin{matrix}2&0&0\\2&k&2\\5&2&k\end{matrix}\right|=0$ (first row is $\overrightarrow{BA}=(2,0,0)$).
Expanding along the first row: $2(k^2-4)=0$, so $k=\pm2$.
For $k=2$: directions $(2,2,2)$ and $(5,2,2)$ have cross product $(0,6,-6)\parallel(0,1,-1)$, so the normal is $\hat j-\hat k$.
The plane is $y-z=\lambda$; it passes through $(1,-1,0)$, so $\lambda=-1$ and the plane is $y-z=-1$, option (C).
For $k=-2$: directions $(2,-2,2)$ and $(5,2,-2)$ have cross product $(0,14,14)\parallel(0,1,1)$, so the normal is $\hat j+\hat k$.
The plane is $y+z=\lambda$; through $(1,-1,0)$ it gives $\lambda=-1$, so $y+z=-1$, option (B).
Hence the correct options are (B) and (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: For each option, demand that both lines are parallel to the plane and both base points lie on it; this fixes the allowed $k$.
solution: A plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=-1$ contains a line iff the direction is perpendicular to $\vec n$ and a point of the line lies on it.
Both base points $(1,-1,0)$ and $(-1,-1,0)$ give $y=-1,\ z=0$, so every option $y+pz=-1$ (any $p$) is satisfied by both points.
Direction conditions with $\vec n=(0,1,p)$: $\vec n\cdot(2,k,2)=k+2p=0$ and $\vec n\cdot(5,2,k)=2+pk=0$.
(A) $p=2$: $k=-4$ and $k=-1$ conflict, so (A) fails. (D) $p=-2$: $k=4$ and $k=1$ conflict, so (D) fails.
(B) $p=1$: $k=-2$ and $k=-2$ agree, so (B) works. (C) $p=-1$: $k=2$ and $k=2$ agree, so (C) works.
Hence (B) and (C), with $k=-2$ and $k=2$ respectively.

useful_results: Lines through $A,B$ with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ are coplanar iff $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$; if also $\vec d_1\nparallel\vec d_2$, they intersect.
The plane containing two coplanar non-parallel lines has normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$ and passes through $A$.
A plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=c$ contains the line $A+t\vec d$ iff $\vec n\cdot\vec d=0$ and $\vec n\cdot A=c$ - a quick test for MCQ options.
A parameter appearing in both direction ratios often gives a quadratic in the coplanarity condition (here $k^2=4$), so expect two planes, one per value.

concepts: Diagonals of a parallelogram and scalar triple product (volume of parallelepiped)
questions.question: Let $\overrightarrow{PR}=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{SQ}=\hat i-3\hat j-4\hat k$ determine diagonals of a parallelogram $PQRS$ and $\overrightarrow{PT}=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$ be another vector. Then the volume of the parallelepiped determined by the vectors $\overrightarrow{PT},\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS}$ is:
questions.key_idea: With $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec a,\ \overrightarrow{PS}=\vec b$ the diagonals are $\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec a-\vec b$, so $\vec a,\vec b$ follow by adding and subtracting.
solution: Let $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vec a$ and $\overrightarrow{QR}=\overrightarrow{PS}=\vec b$. Then $\overrightarrow{PR}=\vec a+\vec b$ and $\overrightarrow{SQ}=\vec a-\vec b$.
So $\vec a=\frac{\overrightarrow{PR}+\overrightarrow{SQ}}{2}$ and $\vec b=\frac{\overrightarrow{PR}-\overrightarrow{SQ}}{2}$.
$\vec a=\frac{(4,-2,-6)}{2}=2\hat i-\hat j-3\hat k$ and $\vec b=\frac{(2,4,2)}{2}=\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$.
Volume $=|\overrightarrow{PT}\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)|$, the absolute value of the determinant with rows $\vec a,\ \vec b,\ \overrightarrow{PT}$.
The volume is $10$ cubic units.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\vec a\times\vec b=-\frac12\,\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{SQ}$ so the volume comes straight from the given diagonals.
solution: With $\vec a=\overrightarrow{PQ},\ \vec b=\overrightarrow{PS}$: $\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{SQ}=(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec a=-2\,\vec a\times\vec b$.
So $|[\overrightarrow{PT}\ \vec a\ \vec b]|=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{PT}\cdot(\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{SQ})\right|$.
Volume $=\frac12|-20|=10$.

useful_results: For a parallelogram with sides $\vec a,\vec b$ the diagonals are $\vec a\pm\vec b$, and $(\vec a+\vec b)\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-2\,\vec a\times\vec b$, hence area $=\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$.
Volume of the parallelepiped on $\vec x,\vec y,\vec z$ is $|\vec x\cdot(\vec y\times\vec z)|$, the absolute value of the determinant of their components; order only changes the sign.
Sides from diagonals: $\vec a=\frac{\vec d_1+\vec d_2}{2},\ \vec b=\frac{\vec d_1-\vec d_2}{2}$ when $\vec d_1=\vec a+\vec b,\ \vec d_2=\vec a-\vec b$ (check the orientation of the given diagonals).
So here the volume needs only $\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{SQ}=(-10,10,-10)$, with no need to find the sides: $\frac12|-20|=10$.

concepts: Coplanarity of vectors
Combinations (selection of vectors)
questions.question: Consider the set of eight vectors $V=\{a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k:\ a,b,c\in\{-1,1\}\}$. Three non-coplanar vectors can be chosen from $V$ in $2^p$ ways. Then $p$ is:
questions.key_idea: Three of these vectors are coplanar exactly when two of them are collinear (an antipodal pair); count and subtract those triples.
solution: The eight vectors $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$ are the position vectors of the vertices of a cube centred at the origin $O$.
Total ways to choose three vectors: $^8C_3=56$.

Three vectors are coplanar if two of them are collinear. Collinear pairs are the antipodal pairs $\overrightarrow{OA},\overrightarrow{OR}$; $\overrightarrow{OB},\overrightarrow{OS}$; $\overrightarrow{OC},\overrightarrow{OP}$; $\overrightarrow{OD},\overrightarrow{OQ}$ - 4 pairs.
For each pair, the third vector can be any of the remaining $6$, giving $4\times6=24$ coplanar triples (no triple contains two such pairs).
Any other triple has no antipodal pair. A plane through $O$ spanned by two non-antipodal vectors holds only $4$ of the vectors (two antipodal pairs), so the third is off it.
Number of non-coplanar triples $=\,^8C_3-4\cdot6=56-24=32$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Count ordered selections: each new vector must avoid the plane already spanned, then divide by $3!$.
solution: Pick the first vector in $8$ ways.
The second must not be $\pm$ the first: $8-2=6$ ways.
The first two (non-collinear) span a plane through $O$. Such a plane contains exactly $4$ of the $8$ vectors (two antipodal pairs), e.g. the plane $x=y$ contains $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$ with $a=b$.
So the third vector can be chosen in $8-4=4$ ways.
Ordered triples: $8\times6\times4=192$; unordered: $\frac{192}{3!}=32=2^5$, so $p=5$.

useful_results: Three non-zero vectors are coplanar iff $\left|\begin{matrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{matrix}\right|=0$; if two are parallel they are automatically coplanar.

For the vectors $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, any plane through $O$ spanned by two non-antipodal ones contains exactly $4$ of them, so every coplanar triple contains an antipodal pair (checked by listing all $56$ triples: $24$ coplanar).
Same cube, vertices as points: $^8C_4=70$ four-sets, of which $12$ are coplanar ($6$ faces $+\ 6$ diagonal planes), so $58$ tetrahedra.
Counting non-coplanar selections: subtract coplanar cases by structure (collinear pair, same plane) instead of testing each triple.

concepts: Foot of the perpendicular on a plane and projection of a line on a plane
questions.question: Perpendiculars are drawn from points on the line $\frac{x+2}{2}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z}{3}$ to the plane $x+y+z=3$. The feet of perpendiculars lie on the line:
questions.key_idea: The feet of the perpendiculars form the projection of the line on the plane, whose direction is $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.
solution: A point on the line is $(2t-2,\,-t-1,\,3t)$. Let its foot on the plane be $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$; the perpendicular has direction $(1,1,1)$.
So $\frac{\alpha-2t+2}{1}=\frac{\beta+t+1}{1}=\frac{\gamma-3t}{1}=k$, giving $\alpha=k+2t-2,\ \beta=k-t-1,\ \gamma=k+3t$.
The foot lies on the plane: $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3$, so $3k+4t-3=3$ and $k=\frac{6-4t}{3}$.
Eliminating $t$: $\frac{3\alpha}{2}=\frac{3\beta-3}{-7}=\frac{3\gamma-6}{5}$, i.e. $\frac{\alpha}{2}=\frac{\beta-1}{-7}=\frac{\gamma-2}{5}$.
So the feet lie on $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-7}=\frac{z-2}{5}$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: The locus of feet is the orthogonal projection of the line on the plane: direction $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$, through the point where the line meets the plane.
solution: The line has direction $\vec d=(2,-1,3)$; the plane normal is $\vec n=(1,1,1)$ with $|\vec n|^2=3$.
Projected direction: $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{3}\vec n=(2,-1,3)-\frac43(1,1,1)=\left(\frac23,-\frac73,\frac53\right)\parallel(2,-7,5)$.
The line meets the plane where $(2t-2)+(-t-1)+3t=3$, i.e. $4t=6$, $t=\frac32$, at $\left(1,-\frac52,\frac92\right)$; this point is its own foot.
So the foot-line is $\left(1,-\frac52,\frac92\right)+s(2,-7,5)$. At $s=-\frac12$ it passes through $(0,1,2)$.
Hence the line is $\frac{x}{2}=\frac{y-1}{-7}=\frac{z-2}{5}$, option (D).

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=c$ is $P-\frac{\vec n\cdot P-c}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$.

The projection of the line $A+t\vec d$ on the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec r=c$ is the line through the foot of $A$ with direction $\vec d-\frac{\vec d\cdot\vec n}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$ (a point if $\vec d\parallel\vec n$).
If the line meets the plane, that intersection point lies on the projection; if the line is parallel to the plane, its projection is a parallel line (same direction $\vec d$) lying in the plane.
Option checking: the projection direction must satisfy $\vec d'\cdot\vec n=0$ (here $2-7+5=0$), but options can share this property (e.g. (A): $5+8-13=0$), so also test a point of the foot-line.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Cross product (common perpendicular) and lines in 3D
Distance between two points
questions.question: A line $l$ passing through the origin is perpendicular to the lines $l_1:(3+t)\hat i+(-1+2t)\hat j+(4+2t)\hat k,\ -\infty<t<\infty$ and $l_2:(3+2s)\hat i+(3+2s)\hat j+(2+s)\hat k,\ -\infty<s<\infty$. Then the coordinate(s) of the point(s) on $l_2$ at a distance of $\sqrt{17}$ from the point of intersection of $l$ and $l_1$ is (are):
questions.key_idea: The direction of $l$ is $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; its meeting point with $l_1$ then fixes the point $P$ from which distances on $l_2$ are measured.
solution: A vector perpendicular to both is $\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&2&2\\2&2&1\end{matrix}\right|=-2\hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k$.
So $l:\ \vec r=\lambda(-2,3,-2)$, since it passes through the origin.
Intersection of $l$ and $l_1$: $3+t=-2\lambda$, $-1+2t=3\lambda$, $4+2t=-2\lambda$.
Subtracting the first from the third gives $1+t=0$, so $t=-1$, $\lambda=-1$ (and the second equation $-3=-3$ checks).
The point of intersection is $P(2,-3,2)$.
$s=-2$ gives $(-1,-1,0)$, option (B); $s=-\frac{10}{9}$ gives $\left(\frac79,\frac79,\frac89\right)$, option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: A line through $O$ that meets $l_1$ at right angles meets it at the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $l_1$, so no cross product is needed.
solution: Since $l$ passes through $O$, meets $l_1$ and is perpendicular to it, the meeting point $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $l_1$.
Hence $P=(2,-3,2)$, the same point as before.
Points of $l_2$ at distance $\sqrt{17}$ from $P$: $9s^2+28s+20=0$, so $s=-2,-\frac{10}{9}$.

These give $(-1,-1,0)$ and $\left(\frac79,\frac79,\frac89\right)$, options (B) and (D). Options (A) at $s=-\frac13$ and (C) at $s=-1$ lie on $l_2$ but are at squared distances $\frac{258}{9}$ and $18$, so they fail.

solution: $L_1:\ \frac{x-5}{0}=\frac{y}{3-\alpha}=\frac{z}{-2}$ passes through $(5,0,0)$.
$L_2:\ \frac{x-\alpha}{0}=\frac{y}{-1}=\frac{z}{2-\alpha}$ passes through $(\alpha,0,0)$.
Coplanarity: $\left|\begin{matrix}5-\alpha&0&0\\0&3-\alpha&-2\\0&-1&2-\alpha\end{matrix}\right|=0$ (the first row is the difference of the points, the other two are the directions).
Expanding: $(5-\alpha)\left[(3-\alpha)(2-\alpha)-2\right]=0$.
$(3-\alpha)(2-\alpha)-2=\alpha^2-5\alpha+4$, so $(5-\alpha)(\alpha^2-5\alpha+4)=0$.

questions.question: Let $\vec x,\vec y$ and $\vec z$ be three vectors each of magnitude $\sqrt2$ and the angle between each pair of them is $\frac\pi3$. If $\vec a$ is a nonzero vector perpendicular to $\vec x$ and $\vec y\times\vec z$, and $\vec b$ is a nonzero vector perpendicular to $\vec y$ and $\vec z\times\vec x$, then:

solution: Each vector has length $\sqrt2$ and the angle between each pair is $\frac\pi3$, so $\vec x\cdot\vec y=\vec y\cdot\vec z=\vec z\cdot\vec x=\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2\cos\frac\pi3=1$ and $\vec x\cdot\vec x=\vec y\cdot\vec y=\vec z\cdot\vec z=2$.
$\vec a\perp\vec x$ and $\vec a\perp(\vec y\times\vec z)$, so $\vec a\parallel\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z=\vec y-\vec z$.
Hence $\vec a=\lambda_1(\vec y-\vec z)$ ... (1).
Dot with $\vec y$: $\vec a\cdot\vec y=\lambda_1(\vec y\cdot\vec y-\vec y\cdot\vec z)=\lambda_1(2-1)=\lambda_1$ ... (2).

From (1) and (2): $\vec a=(\vec a\cdot\vec y)(\vec y-\vec z)$. So (B) is true. As $\vec a
eq\vec 0$ we have $\vec a\cdot\vec y
eq0$, and $\vec y-\vec z
eq\vec z-\vec y$, so (D) is false.
Similarly $\vec b\parallel\vec y\times(\vec z\times\vec x)=(\vec y\cdot\vec x)\vec z-(\vec y\cdot\vec z)\vec x=\vec z-\vec x$, so $\vec b=\lambda_2(\vec z-\vec x)$.
Dot with $\vec z$: $\vec b\cdot\vec z=\lambda_2(2-1)=\lambda_2$, so $\vec b=(\vec b\cdot\vec z)(\vec z-\vec x)$: (A) is true.
Now $\vec a\cdot\vec b=(\vec a\cdot\vec y)(\vec b\cdot\vec z)\,(\vec y-\vec z)\cdot(\vec z-\vec x)$.
$(\vec y-\vec z)\cdot(\vec z-\vec x)=\vec y\cdot\vec z-\vec y\cdot\vec x-\vec z\cdot\vec z+\vec z\cdot\vec x=1-1-2+1=-1$.
So $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-(\vec a\cdot\vec y)(\vec b\cdot\vec z)$: (C) is true. Answer: (A), (B), (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: A vector perpendicular to $\vec y\times\vec z$ lies in the plane of $\vec y,\vec z$; then one dot product with $\vec x$ fixes it.
solution: $\vec a\perp(\vec y\times\vec z)$ means $\vec a$ lies in the plane of $\vec y$ and $\vec z$, so $\vec a=\alpha\vec y+\beta\vec z$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec x=0$ gives $\alpha(\vec y\cdot\vec x)+\beta(\vec z\cdot\vec x)=\alpha+\beta=0$, so $\vec a=\alpha(\vec y-\vec z)$ with $\alpha\neq0$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec y=\alpha(2-1)=\alpha$, hence $\vec a=(\vec a\cdot\vec y)(\vec y-\vec z)$: (B) true, (D) false.
$\vec b\perp(\vec z\times\vec x)$ means $\vec b=\gamma\vec z+\delta\vec x$; $\vec b\cdot\vec y=\gamma+\delta=0$, so $\vec b=\gamma(\vec z-\vec x)$.
$\vec b\cdot\vec z=\gamma(2-1)=\gamma$, hence $\vec b=(\vec b\cdot\vec z)(\vec z-\vec x)$: (A) true.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b=\alpha\gamma(\vec y-\vec z)\cdot(\vec z-\vec x)=\alpha\gamma(1-1-2+1)=-\alpha\gamma=-(\vec a\cdot\vec y)(\vec b\cdot\vec z)$: (C) true.
No triple-product expansion was needed. Answer: (A), (B), (C).

Summing $n-1$ equal terms, $|\mathrm{Im}|=|\mathrm{Re}|$ means $\left|\tan\frac{2\pi}n\right|=1$, so $\frac{2\pi}n=\frac\pi4$ ($n=8$) or $\frac{3\pi}4$ ($n=\frac83$, not an integer): B-r.
C: The normal at $(x_1,y_1)$ of $\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac{y^2}{3}=1$ is $\frac{6x}{x_1}-\frac{3y}{y_1}=6-3=3$. At $(h,1)$ its slope is $\frac{6/h}{3}=\frac2h$.
A line perpendicular to $x+y=8$ (slope $-1$) has slope $1$, so $\frac2h=1$, $h=2$ (and $(2,1)$ is on the ellipse): C-q.
D: $\cot$ of the left side is $\frac{(2x+1)(4x+1)-1}{(2x+1)+(4x+1)}=\frac{8x^2+6x}{6x+2}=\frac{x(4x+3)}{3x+1}$, and $\cot\left(\tan^{-1}\frac2{x^2}\right)=\frac{x^2}2$.
So $\frac{x^2}2=\frac{x(4x+3)}{3x+1}$, i.e. $x(3x+1)=2(4x+3)$, $3x^2-7x-6=0$: the only positive root is $x=3$, one solution: D-p.
Check: $\tan^{-1}\frac17+\tan^{-1}\frac1{13}=\tan^{-1}\frac29$ and $\frac2{x^2}=\frac29$. So option (A).

useful_results: Chebyshev: $\cos(n\cos^{-1}x)=T_n(x)$ satisfies $(1-x^2)y''-xy'+n^2y=0$, so $(x^2-1)y''+xy'=n^2y$ for any $n$ (here $n=3$, value $9$).

For a regular $n$-gon centred at the origin, consecutive position vectors subtend $\frac{2\pi}n$: $\vec a_k\cdot\vec a_{k+1}=r^2\cos\frac{2\pi}n$ and $|\vec a_k\times\vec a_{k+1}|=r^2\sin\frac{2\pi}n$, with the same direction for all $k$ in one orientation.
Normal to $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ at $(x_1,y_1)$: $\frac{a^2x}{x_1}-\frac{b^2y}{y_1}=a^2-b^2$; the tangent at $(x_1,y_1)$ is perpendicular to this normal.
$\tan^{-1}u+\tan^{-1}v=\tan^{-1}\frac{u+v}{1-uv}$ only when $uv<1$ (for $u,v>0$); for $u,v>0$ with $uv>1$ add $\pi$. Here $uv=\frac1{(2x+1)(4x+1)}<1$ for $x>0$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point to a line in 3D and perpendicular lines
questions.question: From a point $P(\lambda,\lambda,\lambda)$, perpendiculars $PQ$ and $PR$ are drawn respectively on the lines $y=x,\ z=1$ and $y=-x,\ z=-1$. If $P$ is such that $\angle QPR$ is a right angle, then the possible value(s) of $\lambda$ is(are)
questions.key_idea: $PQ\perp PR$ gives $\lambda=\pm1$, but $\lambda=1$ puts $P$ on a line, so reject it.
solution: The line $y=x,\ z=1$ is $\frac x1=\frac y1=\frac{z-1}0=\alpha$, so $Q=(\alpha,\alpha,1)$ and the direction ratios of $PQ$ are $\lambda-\alpha,\ \lambda-\alpha,\ \lambda-1$.
$PQ$ is perpendicular to the line (direction $(1,1,0)$): $(\lambda-\alpha)+(\lambda-\alpha)+0=0$, so $\alpha=\lambda$.
Hence $Q=(\lambda,\lambda,1)$ and the direction ratios of $PQ$ are $0,\ 0,\ \lambda-1$.
The line $y=-x,\ z=-1$ is $\frac x{-1}=\frac y1=\frac{z+1}0=\beta$, so $R=(-\beta,\beta,-1)$ and the direction ratios of $PR$ are $\lambda+\beta,\ \lambda-\beta,\ \lambda+1$.
$PR$ is perpendicular to this line (direction $(-1,1,0)$): $-(\lambda+\beta)+(\lambda-\beta)=0$, so $\beta=0$.
Hence $R=(0,0,-1)$ and the direction ratios of $PR$ are $\lambda,\ \lambda,\ \lambda+1$.
$PQ\perp PR$: $0+0+(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)=0$, so $\lambda=\pm1$.
For $\lambda=1$, $P=(1,1,1)$ lies on the line $y=x,\ z=1$, so $Q=P$ and $PQ$ is not a line: this value is rejected.
For $\lambda=-1$: $P=(-1,-1,-1)$, $Q=(-1,-1,1)$, $R=(0,0,-1)$; $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=(0,0,2)\cdot(1,1,0)=0$. So $\lambda=-1$: option (C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the first condition as 1-alpha+lambda-alpha+0=0 (it should be (lambda-alpha)+(lambda-alpha)+0=0), says 'PQ is perpendicular to (2)' where PR is meant, and ends with a stray '1 = -1'. Corrected these three slips; the working otherwise and the answer (C) are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Project $P$ onto the planes $z=\pm1$ containing the lines, read off $Q,R$, and use $QR^2=PQ^2+PR^2$ for the right angle.
solution: The line $y=x,\ z=1$ lies in the plane $z=1$. The projection of $P$ on that plane is $(\lambda,\lambda,1)$, which already lies on $y=x$, so $Q=(\lambda,\lambda,1)$ (three perpendiculars).
The line $y=-x,\ z=-1$ lies in $z=-1$. The projection of $P$ is $(\lambda,\lambda,-1)$; its foot on $y=-x$ in that plane is $(0,0,-1)$, so $R=(0,0,-1)$.
$\angle QPR=90^\circ$ iff $QR^2=PQ^2+PR^2$.
$QR^2=\lambda^2+\lambda^2+2^2=2\lambda^2+4$, $PQ^2=(\lambda-1)^2$, $PR^2=2\lambda^2+(\lambda+1)^2$.
So $2\lambda^2+4=(\lambda-1)^2+(\lambda+1)^2+2\lambda^2=4\lambda^2+2$, giving $\lambda^2=1$.
$\lambda=1$ puts $P$ on the first line (then $Q=P$, degenerate), so $\lambda=-1$: option (C).

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $A+t\vec d$ is $A+\frac{(P-A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$; if the line lies in a coordinate plane, first project $P$ onto that plane.
$\angle QPR=90^\circ\iff\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=0\iff QR^2=PQ^2+PR^2\iff P$ is on the sphere with diameter $QR$.
Always test the roots: when $P$ lies on the line, the 'perpendicular' $PQ$ has zero length and the angle $QPR$ is undefined.
Here $P=(\lambda,\lambda,\lambda)$ moves on the line $x=y=z$, and the feet $Q=(\lambda,\lambda,1)$, $R=(0,0,-1)$ are found with the same two perpendicularity conditions.

concepts: Linear combination of non-coplanar vectors (components along vectors)
questions.question: Suppose that $\vec p,\vec q$ and $\vec r$ are three non-coplanar vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let the components of a vector $\vec s$ along $\vec p,\vec q$ and $\vec r$ be $4,3$ and $5$ respectively. If the components of this vector $\vec s$ along $(-\vec p+\vec q+\vec r)$, $(\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)$ and $(-\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)$ are $x,y$ and $z$ respectively, then the value of $2x+y+z$ is
questions.key_idea: Equate coefficients of the independent $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ in the two expressions of $\vec s$.
solution: Components along $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are $4,3,5$, so $\vec s=4\vec p+3\vec q+5\vec r$.
Also $\vec s=x(-\vec p+\vec q+\vec r)+y(\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)+z(-\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)$.
Compare coefficients of $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ (non-coplanar, so independent): $-x+y-z=4$ ... (1), $x-y-z=3$ ... (2), $x+y+z=5$ ... (3).

alternate_solutions.idea: Express $2x+y+z$ directly as a combination of the three equations; no need to find $x,y,z$ separately.
solution: The equations are $E_1:-x+y-z=4$, $E_2:x-y-z=3$, $E_3:x+y+z=5$.
Seek $u,v,w$ with $uE_1+vE_2+wE_3$ having coefficients $(2,1,1)$: $-u+v+w=2$, $u-v+w=1$, $-u-v+w=1$.
Adding the first two: $2w=3$, so $w=\frac32$. Subtracting the third from the first: $2v=1$, so $v=\frac12$. Then the second gives $u=v-w+1=0$.
So $2x+y+z=0\cdot E_1+\frac12E_2+\frac32E_3$, whose right side is $\frac12\cdot3+\frac32\cdot5=9$.

useful_results: If $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are non-coplanar, every vector has a unique expression $\alpha\vec p+\beta\vec q+\gamma\vec r$, so two expressions can be compared coefficient by coefficient.

The new vectors $(-\vec p+\vec q+\vec r)$, $(\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)$, $(-\vec p-\vec q+\vec r)$ are again non-coplanar: the coefficient determinant is $-4\neq0$ (volume multiplies by $4$ in magnitude), so $x,y,z$ are unique.
'Component along $\vec p$' here means the coefficient of $\vec p$ in the decomposition, not an orthogonal projection (which would need dot products).
A target such as $2x+y+z$ can be obtained as a combination of the equations, saving the full solve; check: $\frac12\cdot3+\frac32\cdot5=9$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Vector algebra in a triangle (scalar and vector products)
questions.question: Let $\triangle PQR$ be a triangle. Let $\vec a=\overrightarrow{QR}$, $\vec b=\overrightarrow{RP}$ and $\vec c=\overrightarrow{PQ}$. If $|\vec a|=12$, $|\vec b|=4\sqrt3$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c=24$, then which of the following is (are) true?
questions.key_idea: $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$ gives $|\vec c|$, $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ and $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec c\times\vec a$.
solution: Going round the triangle, $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$, so $\vec b+\vec c=-\vec a$.
Square: $|\vec b|^2+|\vec c|^2+2\vec b\cdot\vec c=|\vec a|^2$, i.e. $48+|\vec c|^2+48=144$, so $|\vec c|^2=48$ and $|\vec c|=4\sqrt3$.
$\vec a+\vec b=-\vec c$: $|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+2\vec a\cdot\vec b=|\vec c|^2$, i.e. $144+48+2\vec a\cdot\vec b=48$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=-72$: (D) true.
Cross $\vec a$ with $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$: $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec a\times\vec c=\vec0$, so $\vec c\times\vec a=\vec a\times\vec b$.
Then $|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec c\times\vec a|=2|\vec a\times\vec b|=2\sqrt{|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}$.
$=2\sqrt{144\cdot48-72^2}=2\sqrt{1728}=2\cdot24\sqrt3=48\sqrt3$: (C) true.
Answer: (A), (C), (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Solve the triangle itself: the sides are $12,4\sqrt3,4\sqrt3$ with $\angle P=120^\circ$; then dot and cross products are read from angle and area.
solution: $\vec b\cdot\vec c=\overrightarrow{RP}\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ}=-|PR||PQ|\cos P=24$, and the cosine rule gives $QR^2=PR^2+PQ^2-2\,PR\cdot PQ\cos P=48+PQ^2+48$.
With $QR=12$: $PQ^2=48$, so $PQ=4\sqrt3=PR$ and the triangle is isosceles.
$\cos P=\frac{48+48-144}{2\cdot48}=-\frac12$, so $P=120^\circ$ and $Q=R=30^\circ$.
$\vec a=\overrightarrow{QR}$ and $\vec b=\overrightarrow{RP}$ are head-to-tail, so the angle between them is $180^\circ-R=150^\circ$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=12\cdot4\sqrt3\cos150^\circ=-72$: (D) true.
Area $\triangle=\frac12\cdot48\sin120^\circ=12\sqrt3$. For head-to-tail sides, $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec b\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec a$ has magnitude $2\triangle=24\sqrt3$.
So $|\vec a\times\vec b+\vec c\times\vec a|=2\cdot24\sqrt3=48\sqrt3$: (C) true. Answer (A), (C), (D).

useful_results: If $\vec a+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$ (sides taken head to tail), then $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec b\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec a$, with magnitude $2\times$ area of the triangle.

$\vec a\cdot\vec b=\frac{|\vec c|^2-|\vec a|^2-|\vec b|^2}{2}=-|\vec a||\vec b|\cos C$ for head-to-tail sides (interior angle $C$ is the supplement of the angle between the vectors). Here $\frac{48-144-48}2=-72$.
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ (here $6912-5184=1728$).
Squaring $\vec u+\vec v=-\vec w$ is the vector form of the cosine rule; always check the sign convention ($\overrightarrow{QR},\overrightarrow{RP},\overrightarrow{PQ}$ are head to tail).

concepts: Family of planes through the line of intersection and distance of a point from a plane
questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, consider the planes $P_1: y=0$ and $P_2: x+z=1$. Let $P_3$ be a plane, different from $P_1$ and $P_2$, which passes through the intersection of $P_1$ and $P_2$. If the distance of the point $(0,1,0)$ from $P_3$ is $1$ and the distance of a point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ from $P_3$ is $2$, then which of the following relations is (are) true?
questions.key_idea: Planes through the line $P_1\cap P_2$ form the pencil $x+z-1+\lambda y=0$; one distance condition fixes $\lambda$.
solution: Any plane through the intersection of $P_1: y=0$ and $P_2: x+z-1=0$ is $(x+z-1)+\lambda y=0$, i.e. $x+\lambda y+z-1=0$.
The distance of $(0,1,0)$ from it is $1$: $\frac{|0+\lambda+0-1|}{\sqrt{1+\lambda^2+1}}=1$.
Squaring: $(\lambda-1)^2=\lambda^2+2$, so $-2\lambda=1$ and $\lambda=-\frac12$.
The distance of $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ from $P_3$ is $2$: $\frac{|2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-2|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}}=2$, i.e. $|2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-2|=6$.
So $2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-2=6$ or $-6$, i.e. $2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-8=0$ (D) or $2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma+4=0$ (B).
Options (A) and (C) have $+\beta$ and are not of this form. Answer: (B), (D).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's line 'Dist. from (alpha, beta, gamma) is 3' should read 2 (the question gives 2; the next line correctly uses 2 on the right side and 3 as the denominator). Steps were also filled in. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Planes through the line $P_1\cap P_2$ at distance $1$ from $M(0,1,0)$ are tangent to the unit sphere at $M$; the second one is the mirror image of $P_1$ in the plane through the line and $M$.
solution: $P_1\cap P_2$ is the line $\ell$ through $A(1,0,0)$ and $B(0,0,1)$. $M(0,1,0)$ is at distance $1$ from $P_1$, so $P_1$ is one such plane.
The two planes through $\ell$ tangent to the unit sphere centred at $M$ are mirror images in the plane through $\ell$ and $M$, which is $x+y+z=1$ (it contains $A,B,M$), normal $\vec m=(1,1,1)$.
Reflect the normal $\vec n_1=(0,1,0)$ of $P_1$: $\vec n_3=\vec n_1-\frac{2\,\vec n_1\cdot\vec m}{|\vec m|^2}\vec m=(0,1,0)-\frac23(1,1,1)=\left(-\frac23,\frac13,-\frac23\right)\parallel(2,-1,2)$.
$P_3$ contains $A$: $2x-y+2z=2$.
Distance $2$ from $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$: $|2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-2|=2\cdot3=6$, giving (D) $2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma-8=0$ and (B) $2\alpha-\beta+2\gamma+4=0$.

useful_results: Planes through the line $P_1=0,\ P_2=0$: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$ (all except $P_2$) or $P_2+\lambda P_1=0$ (all except $P_1$).
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz+d=0$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0+d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; setting it equal to $k$ gives two parallel planes (the $\pm$ cases).
Through a line outside a sphere there are exactly two tangent planes; they are mirror images in the plane through the line and the centre.
Reflection of a direction $\vec n$ in a plane with normal $\vec m$: $\vec n-\frac{2(\vec n\cdot\vec m)}{|\vec m|^2}\vec m$ (here it gives $(2,-1,2)$ up to scale, matching $\lambda=-\frac12$).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Line parallel to planes, foot of perpendicular and locus in 3D
questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $L$ be a straight line passing through the origin. Suppose that all the points on $L$ are at a constant distance from the two planes $P_1: x+2y-z+1=0$ and $P_2: 2x-y+z-1=0$. Let $M$ be the locus of the feet of the perpendiculars drawn from the points on $L$ to the plane $P_1$. Which of the following points lie(s) on $M$?
questions.key_idea: Constant distance from both planes means $L\parallel\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$; the feet then form a line.
solution: All points of $L$ are at constant distance from $P_1$ and $P_2$, so $L$ is parallel to both planes. Its direction is $\vec v=(\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k)\times(2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$.
$\vec v=\hat i(2-1)-\hat j(1+2)+\hat k(-1-4)=\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k$.
$L$ passes through the origin, so a general point of $L$ is $A(\lambda,-3\lambda,-5\lambda)$.
Foot $(h,k,l)$ of the perpendicular from $A$ to $P_1$ (normal $(1,2,-1)$): $\frac{h-\lambda}1=\frac{k+3\lambda}2=\frac{l+5\lambda}{-1}=-\frac{\lambda-6\lambda+5\lambda+1}{1+4+1}=-\frac16$.
So $h=\lambda-\frac16$, $k=-3\lambda-\frac13$, $l=-5\lambda+\frac16$.
$M$ is the line through $\left(-\frac16,-\frac13,\frac16\right)$ with direction $(1,-3,-5)$.
(A): $\lambda=\frac16$ gives $\left(0,-\frac56,-\frac23\right)$: on $M$. (B): $\lambda=0$ gives $\left(-\frac16,-\frac13,\frac16\right)$: on $M$.
(C): $h=-\frac56$ needs $\lambda=-\frac23$, then $k=2-\frac13=\frac53\neq0$: not on $M$.
(D): $h=-\frac13$ needs $\lambda=-\frac16$, then $k=\frac12-\frac13=\frac16\neq0$: not on $M$. Answer: (A), (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: $M$ is the projection of $L$ on $P_1$: the intersection of $P_1$ with the plane through $L$ perpendicular to $P_1$; test each point in two plane equations.
solution: As $L\parallel P_1$, its projection $M$ is a line lying in $P_1$ and in the plane $\Pi$ through $L$ perpendicular to $P_1$.
$\Pi$ contains $\vec v=(1,-3,-5)$ and $\vec n_1=(1,2,-1)$ as directions and passes through $O$, so its normal is $\vec v\times\vec n_1=(13,-4,5)$ and $\Pi:13x-4y+5z=0$.
(B): $-\frac16-\frac23-\frac16+1=0$ and $-\frac{13}6+\frac43+\frac56=0$: on $M$.
(C): $-\frac56+0-\frac16+1=0$ but $13\left(-\frac56\right)+5\cdot\frac16=-10\neq0$: not on $M$.
(D): $-\frac13+0-\frac23+1=0$ but $13\left(-\frac13\right)+5\cdot\frac23=-1\neq0$: not on $M$. Answer: (A), (B).

useful_results: A line has constant distance from a plane iff it is parallel to it; parallel to two planes iff its direction is $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $\vec n\cdot\vec r+d=0$ is $A-\frac{\vec n\cdot A+d}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$. Here $\vec n\cdot A=0$ on $L$, so the foot is always $A-\frac16\vec n$.
The projection of a line parallel to a plane onto that plane is a parallel line; it is the intersection of the plane with the plane through the line perpendicular to it (normal $\vec v\times\vec n$).
All four options lie on $P_1$ (check: each satisfies $x+2y-z+1=0$), so the real test is the second condition, e.g. $13x-4y+5z=0$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Dot and cross product of vectors: equality case of $\hat w\cdot(\hat u\times\vec v)$
questions.question: Let $\hat u=u_1\hat i+u_2\hat j+u_3\hat k$ be a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $\hat w=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k)$. Given that there exists a vector $\vec v$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ such that $|\hat u\times\vec v|=1$ and $\hat w\cdot(\hat u\times\vec v)=1$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
options: There is exactly one choice for such $\vec v$
There are infinitely many choices for such $\vec v$
If $\hat u$ lies in the $xy$-plane then $|u_1|=|u_2|$
If $\hat u$ lies in the $xz$-plane then $2|u_1|=|u_3|$
questions.key_idea: $\hat w\cdot(\hat u\times\vec v)=1$ with unit vectors on both sides forces $\hat u\times\vec v=\hat w$.
solution: Since $|\hat w|=1$ and $|\hat u\times\vec v|=1$: $\hat w\cdot(\hat u\times\vec v)=|\hat w||\hat u\times\vec v|\cos\alpha=1$ gives $\cos\alpha=1$, where $\alpha$ is the angle between $\hat w$ and $\hat u\times\vec v$.
So $\hat u\times\vec v=\hat w$ (two unit vectors with $\alpha=0$). A cross product is perpendicular to both factors, hence $\hat w\perp\hat u$ and $\hat w\perp\vec v$.
Such a $\vec v$ exists, so $\hat w$ must be perpendicular to $\hat u$: $\hat u\cdot\hat w=0$, i.e. $u_1+u_2+2u_3=0$.
If $\vec v_0$ is one solution, then $\vec v_0+t\hat u$ also satisfies $\hat u\times(\vec v_0+t\hat u)=\hat w$ for every real $t$. So there are infinitely many choices: (A) false, (B) true.
(C) $\hat u$ in the $xy$-plane means $u_3=0$. Then $u_1+u_2=0$, so $|u_1|=|u_2|$. True.
(D) $\hat u$ in the $xz$-plane means $u_2=0$. Then $u_1+2u_3=0$, so $|u_1|=2|u_3|$, not $2|u_1|=|u_3|$ (both cannot vanish for a unit vector). False.
Hence the correct statements are (B) and (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometric picture: $\hat u$ must lie on the plane $x+y+2z=0$ through the origin perpendicular to $\hat w$; intersect it with the coordinate planes.
solution: $\hat u\times\vec v=\hat w$ is perpendicular to $\hat u$, so $\hat u\perp\hat w$: $\hat u$ lies in the plane $x+y+2z=0$.
Conversely, for any such $\hat u$ take $\vec v=\hat w\times\hat u$: $\hat u\times(\hat w\times\hat u)=\hat w(\hat u\cdot\hat u)-\hat u(\hat u\cdot\hat w)=\hat w$.
All solutions are $\vec v=\hat w\times\hat u+t\hat u$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}$, an infinite family, so (A) is false and (B) is true.
The $xy$-plane meets $x+y+2z=0$ where $z=0$, $x+y=0$: direction $(1,-1,0)$, so $|u_1|=|u_2|$ and (C) is true.
The $xz$-plane meets it where $y=0$, $x+2z=0$: direction $(2,0,-1)$, so $|u_1|=2|u_3|$.
Test: $\hat u=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(2,0,-1)$ gives $2|u_1|=\frac{4}{\sqrt5}\neq\frac{1}{\sqrt5}=|u_3|$, so (D) is false. Answer (B), (C).

useful_results: Cauchy-Schwarz equality case: for a unit vector $\hat w$ and any $\vec n$, $\hat w\cdot\vec n\le|\vec n|$, with equality iff $\vec n=|\vec n|\hat w$.
A cross product is perpendicular to both factors, so $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec c\neq\vec 0$ is solvable for $\vec v$ only if $\vec c\perp\vec u$.

If $\hat u\perp\hat w$ (unit vectors), then $\vec v=\hat w\times\hat u$ solves $\hat u\times\vec v=\hat w$ because $\hat u\times(\hat w\times\hat u)=\hat w$; the full solution set is $\hat w\times\hat u+t\hat u$.
Scalar triple product: $|\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)|\le|\vec a||\vec b||\vec c|$, with equality iff the three vectors are mutually perpendicular.
