concepts: Plane in vector form and reflection of a point in a plane
questions.question: Let $S$ be the reflection of a point $Q$ with respect to the plane given by $\vec r=-(t+p)\hat{i}+t\hat{j}+(1+p)\hat{k}$ where $t,p$ are real parameters and $\hat{i},\hat{j},\hat{k}$ are the unit vectors along the three positive coordinate axes. If the position vectors of $Q$ and $S$ are $10\hat{i}+15\hat{j}+20\hat{k}$ and $\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$ respectively, then which of the following is/are TRUE?
questions.key_idea: The normal of $\vec r=\vec r_0+p\vec u+t\vec v$ is $\vec u\times\vec v$, and the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of $QS$.
solution: $\vec r=\hat{k}+p(-\hat{i}+\hat{k})+t(-\hat{i}+\hat{j})$, a plane through $(0,0,1)$ with direction vectors $(-1,0,1)$ and $(-1,1,0)$.
Normal: $\vec n=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\ -1&0&1\\ -1&1&0\end{vmatrix}=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}-\hat{k}$.
So the plane is $x+y+z=1$ (it passes through $(0,0,1)$).
$Q=(10,15,20)$. The foot of the perpendicular is $F=(10+d,15+d,20+d)$, lying on the plane: $45+3d=1$, so $3d=-44$.
$F$ is the midpoint of $QS$: $\frac{\alpha+10}{2}=10+d$, so $\alpha=10+2d$ and $3\alpha=30-2(44)=-58$.
Similarly $3\beta=45-88=-43$ and $3\gamma=60-88=-28$.
(D) $3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=-58-43-28=-129\neq-121$. False. Answer (A), (B), (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflection in $x+y+z=1$ shifts every coordinate by the same amount $k$; the midpoint condition fixes $k$ and the coordinate sum.
solution: $QS$ is parallel to the normal $(1,1,1)$, so $S=Q+k(1,1,1)$ and $\alpha=10+k$, $\beta=15+k$, $\gamma=20+k$.
The midpoint $Q+\frac{k}{2}(1,1,1)$ lies on $x+y+z=1$: $45+\frac{3k}{2}=1$, so $3k=-88$.
$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=45+3k=-43$, so $3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=-129\neq-121$: (D) false.
$3\gamma=60+3k=-28$, so $3(\alpha+\beta)=3(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-3\gamma=-129+28=-101$: (A) true.

useful_results: For $\vec r=\vec r_0+p\vec u+t\vec v$ the normal is $\vec u\times\vec v$ and the Cartesian equation is $(\vec r-\vec r_0)\cdot(\vec u\times\vec v)=0$.
Reflection of $Q$ in $\vec n\cdot\vec x=d$: $S=Q-\frac{2(\vec n\cdot Q-d)}{|\vec n|^2}\vec n$. Here $n=(1,1,1)$, $d=1$ gives $S=Q-\frac{88}{3}(1,1,1)$.
For the plane $x+y+z=d$, reflection shifts all three coordinates equally, and the coordinate sum $s$ becomes $2d-s$ (here $45\to-43$).
The foot of the perpendicular from $Q$ is the midpoint of $QS$, and $QF=FS$ equals the distance of $Q$ from the plane.

concepts: Shortest distance between lines and distance of a point from a plane in 3D
questions.question:
Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be the lines $\vec r_1=\lambda(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})$ and $\vec r_2=(\hat{j}-\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}+\hat{k})$, respectively. Let $X$ be the set of all the planes $H$ that contain the line $\ell_1$. For a plane $H$, let $d(H)$ denote the smallest possible distance between the points of $\ell_2$ and $H$. Let $H_0$ be a plane in $X$ for which $d(H_0)$ is the maximum value of $d(H)$ as $H$ varies over all planes in $X$. Match each entry in List-I to the correct entries in List-II.
List-I
(P) The value of $d(H_0)$ is
(Q) The distance of the point $(0,1,2)$ from $H_0$ is
(R) The distance of origin from $H_0$ is
(S) The distance of origin from the point of intersection of planes $y=z$, $x=1$ and $H_0$ is
List-II
(1) $\sqrt3$
(2) $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$
(3) $0$
(4) $\sqrt2$
(5) $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$
questions.key_idea: A plane through $\ell_1$ meeting $\ell_2$ has $d=0$, so $H_0$ is the plane through $\ell_1$ parallel to $\ell_2$.
solution: $\ell_1$ passes through the origin with direction $(1,1,1)$; $\ell_2$ passes through $(0,1,-1)$ with direction $(1,0,1)$. They are not parallel.
A plane $H$ through $\ell_1$ that is not parallel to $\ell_2$ meets $\ell_2$, so $d(H)=0$. Hence $d(H)$ is maximum for the plane $H_0$ containing $\ell_1$ and parallel to $\ell_2$.
$H_0$ is $x-z=\lambda'$ and passes through the origin (on $\ell_1$), so $H_0: x-z=0$.
(P) $d(H_0)$ is the distance of $(0,1,-1)$ from $H_0$: $\frac{|0-(-1)|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$. So P $\to$ (5).
(Q) Distance of $(0,1,2)$: $\frac{|0-2|}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$. So Q $\to$ (4).
(R) The origin lies on $H_0$, so the distance is $0$. So R $\to$ (3).
(S) $y=z$, $x=1$ and $x=z$ meet at $(1,1,1)$, whose distance from the origin is $\sqrt3$. So S $\to$ (1).
P $\to$ 5, Q $\to$ 4, R $\to$ 3, S $\to$ 1: option (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: $d(H_0)$ is the shortest distance between the skew lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$, and $\ell_1\subset H_0$ gives (R) and (S) at once.
solution: $\ell_1$: point $\vec 0$, direction $\vec u_1=(1,1,1)$. $\ell_2$: point $(0,1,-1)$, direction $\vec u_2=(1,0,1)$. $\vec u_1\times\vec u_2=(1,0,-1)$ with magnitude $\sqrt2$.

For any $H\supset\ell_1$ and $X\in\ell_2$, $\text{dist}(X,H)\le\text{dist}(X,Y)$ for every $Y\in\ell_1$, so $d(H)\le$ the shortest distance between the lines, with equality for the plane through $\ell_1$ parallel to $\ell_2$.
Shortest distance $=\frac{|(0,1,-1)\cdot(1,0,-1)|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $d(H_0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$: P $\to$ (5).
$H_0$ has normal $(1,0,-1)$ and contains the origin: $x-z=0$. Distance of $(0,1,2)$: $\frac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$: Q $\to$ (4).
The origin is on $\ell_1\subset H_0$, so its distance is $0$: R $\to$ (3).
$(1,1,1)$ is on $\ell_1$ (take $\lambda=1$), hence on $H_0$, and satisfies $y=z$, $x=1$: it is the intersection point, at distance $\sqrt3$: S $\to$ (1). Option (B).

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec a_1+\lambda\vec u_1$ and $\vec a_2+\mu\vec u_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec u_1\times\vec u_2)|}{|\vec u_1\times\vec u_2|}$; here $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

Among planes containing $\ell_1$, the distance to $\ell_2$ is $0$ unless the plane is parallel to $\ell_2$; the maximum equals the skew-line distance and occurs for the plane with normal $\vec u_1\times\vec u_2$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $ax+by+cz=d$ is $\frac{|ax_0+by_0+cz_0-d|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$; for $x-z=0$ and $(0,1,2)$ it is $\sqrt2$.
Any point of a line contained in a plane has distance $0$ from the plane, which settles items like (R) without computation.

concepts: Section formula, coplanarity of points and cross product
questions.question: Let the position vectors of the points $P,Q,R$ and $S$ be $\vec a=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-5\hat{k}$, $\vec b=3\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec c=\frac{17}{5}\hat{i}+\frac{16}{5}\hat{j}+7\hat{k}$ and $\vec d=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, respectively. Then which of the following statements is true?
options: The points $P,Q,R$ and $S$ are NOT coplanar.
$\frac{\vec b+2\vec d}{3}$ is the position vector of a point which divides $PR$ internally in the ratio $5:4$.
$\frac{\vec b+2\vec d}{3}$ is the position vector of a point which divides $PR$ externally in the ratio $5:4$.
The square of the magnitude of the vector $\vec b\times\vec d$ is $95$.
questions.key_idea: Test whether the section point $\frac{\vec b+2\vec d}{3}$ of $QS$ also lies on $PR$ by finding one ratio and checking the other coordinates.
solution: Let this point divide $PR$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$ (from $P$). Equating $x$-coordinates: $\frac{17\lambda}{5}+1=\frac{7}{3}(\lambda+1)$.
$51\lambda+15=35\lambda+35$, so $16\lambda=20$ and $\lambda=\frac54>0$: the division is internal in the ratio $5:4$.

Check the other coordinates: $y=\frac{\frac54\cdot\frac{16}{5}+2}{\frac94}=\frac{6}{9/4}=\frac83$ and $z=\frac{\frac54\cdot7-5}{\frac94}=\frac{15/4}{9/4}=\frac53$. Both match, so (B) is true and (C) is false.
The same point is $Q+\frac23(S-Q)$, so it lies on $QS$ as well as on $PR$. Two lines meeting at a point are coplanar, so (A) is false.
$\vec b\times\vec d=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\ 3&6&3\\ 2&1&1\end{vmatrix}=3\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-9\hat{k}$, so $|\vec b\times\vec d|^2=9+9+81=99\neq95$: (D) is false. Answer (B).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $T-P=t\,(R-P)$ with $T=\frac{\vec b+2\vec d}{3}$, read the ratio from $t$, and use Lagrange's identity for $|\vec b\times\vec d|^2$.
solution: $T=\left(\frac73,\frac83,\frac53\right)$, $\vec{PT}=\left(\frac43,\frac23,\frac{20}{3}\right)$ and $\vec{PR}=\left(\frac{12}{5},\frac65,12\right)$.
$\vec{PT}=\frac59\vec{PR}$: $\frac59\cdot\frac{12}{5}=\frac43$, $\frac59\cdot\frac65=\frac23$, $\frac59\cdot12=\frac{20}{3}$.
So $T$ lies on segment $PR$ with $PT:TR=\frac59:\frac49=5:4$, an internal division: (B) true, (C) false.
$T=Q+\frac23\vec{QS}$ also lies on line $QS$, so lines $PR$ and $QS$ meet and the four points are coplanar: (A) false.
$|\vec b|^2=54$, $|\vec d|^2=6$, $\vec b\cdot\vec d=15$, so $|\vec b\times\vec d|^2=54\cdot6-15^2=324-225=99\neq95$: (D) false. Answer (B).

useful_results: Point dividing $PR$ in ratio $m:n$ internally is $\frac{n\vec p+m\vec r}{m+n}$; externally it is $\frac{m\vec r-n\vec p}{m-n}$. Here $\frac{4\vec a+5\vec c}{9}=\frac13(7,8,5)=\frac{\vec b+2\vec d}{3}$.
Writing $T-P=t(R-P)$ gives the ratio directly: $0<t<1$ means internal, $t>1$ or $t<0$ external, and $PT:TR=t:(1-t)$.
If a section point of $QS$ coincides with a section point of $PR$, the lines intersect and $P,Q,R,S$ are coplanar; in general, coplanarity means $[\vec b-\vec a,\vec c-\vec a,\vec d-\vec a]=0$.
Lagrange's identity $|\vec u\times\vec v|^2=|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2-(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2$ avoids computing the cross product: $54\cdot6-15^2=99$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Locus of points in 3D as a plane and distance between parallel planes
Geometry of rectangles and triangles between parallel planes
questions.question: Let $\mathbb{R}^3$ denote the three-dimensional space. Take two points $P=(1,2,3)$ and $Q=(4,2,7)$. Let $\text{dist}(X,Y)$ denote the distance between two points $X$ and $Y$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Let $S=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^3:(\text{dist}(X,P))^2-(\text{dist}(X,Q))^2=50\}$ and $T=\{Y\in\mathbb{R}^3:(\text{dist}(Y,Q))^2-(\text{dist}(Y,P))^2=50\}$. Then which of the following statements is(are) TRUE?
options: There is a triangle whose area is $1$ and all of whose vertices are from $S$.
There are two distinct points $L$ and $M$ in $T$ such that each point on the line segment $LM$ is also in $T$.
There are infinitely many rectangles of perimeter $48$, two of whose vertices are from $S$ and the other two vertices are from $T$.
There is a square of perimeter $48$, two of whose vertices are from $S$ and the other two vertices are from $T$.
questions.key_idea: $|XP|^2-|XQ|^2=k$ is linear in $X$, so $S$ and $T$ are parallel planes perpendicular to $PQ$, at distance $10$.
solution: $S$: $6x+8z-55=50$, i.e. $6x+8z=105$. $T$: the difference is reversed, so $-(6x+8z-55)=50$, i.e. $6x+8z=5$.
$S$ and $T$ are parallel planes with normal $(6,0,8)$. Distance between them $=\frac{|105-5|}{\sqrt{36+64}}=\frac{100}{10}=10$.
(A) $S$ is a whole plane, so it contains triangles of every area, e.g. the right triangle with legs $\sqrt2,\sqrt2$ lying in $S$ has area $1$. True.
(B) $T$ is a plane, so for any two distinct points $L,M\in T$ the whole segment $LM$ lies in $T$. True.
Rectangle with two vertices on each plane: the two vertices on $S$ cannot be opposite, since the diagonals bisect each other and the common midpoint would lie in both disjoint planes.
So $AB\subset S$ and $CD\subset T$, with $AB=p$ and $AD=BC=q$. $\vec{AD}$ has a component $10$ normal to the planes and an in-plane component $w\perp AB$ of length $t\ge0$.
Hence $q=\sqrt{100+t^2}\ge10$.
(C) Perimeter $48$ means $p+q=24$. For any $q\in[10,24)$ take $p=24-q>0$ and $t=\sqrt{q^2-100}$: this gives infinitely many rectangles. True.
(D) Square: $p=q=12\ge10$, with $t=\sqrt{144-100}=\sqrt{44}$. So a square of perimeter $48$ exists. True. Answer (A), (B), (C), (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the orthonormal frame $\hat n=\frac{(3,0,4)}{5}$, $\hat e_1=(0,1,0)$, $\hat e_2=\frac{(4,0,-3)}{5}$ and construct the rectangles explicitly.
solution: Take $A=\left(\frac{35}{2},0,0\right)\in S$ (since $6\cdot\frac{35}{2}=105$). Moving by $-10\hat n$ lowers $6x+8z$ by $10\cdot10=100$, taking $S$ onto $T$.
For $p>0$, $t\ge0$ let $B=A+p\hat e_1$, $D=A-10\hat n+t\hat e_2$, $C=B+(D-A)$. Then $A,B\in S$ and $C,D\in T$.
$\vec{AB}\cdot\vec{AD}=0$ since $\hat e_1\perp\hat n,\hat e_2$. So $ABCD$ is a rectangle with sides $p$ and $\sqrt{100+t^2}$.
Perimeter $48$: $p+\sqrt{100+t^2}=24$. Every $t\in[0,\sqrt{476})$ gives a positive $p=24-\sqrt{100+t^2}$: infinitely many rectangles, (C) true.
For $t=\sqrt{44}$, $p=24-12=12$ and the other side is $12$: a square of perimeter $48$, (D) true.
(A) $A$, $A+\sqrt2\hat e_1$, $A+\sqrt2\hat e_2$ lie in $S$ and form a right triangle of area $\frac12\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2=1$. (B) $T$ is a plane. Answer (A), (B), (C), (D).

useful_results: $|X-P|^2-|X-Q|^2=k$ is linear in $X$ (the $|X|^2$ terms cancel): the plane $2X\cdot(Q-P)=k+|Q|^2-|P|^2$, perpendicular to $PQ$; $k=0$ gives the perpendicular bisector plane.
The loci for $+k$ and $-k$ are parallel planes at distance $\frac{k}{|PQ|}$; here $\frac{50}{5}=10$ since $|PQ|=\sqrt{9+0+16}=5$.
Distance between parallel planes $ax+by+cz=d_1$ and $=d_2$ is $\frac{|d_1-d_2|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$.
A rectangle with one side in each of two parallel planes at distance $h$ has the slanted side $q=\sqrt{h^2+t^2}\ge h$; if $t=0$ it is perpendicular to the planes.
Two vertices of a rectangle on each of two disjoint parallel planes must be adjacent pairs, because the diagonals share a midpoint.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Line and plane in 3D: intersection, perpendicular line, centroid and perimeter
questions.question: A straight line drawn from the point $P(1,3,2)$, parallel to the line $\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-4}{2}=\frac{z-6}{1}$, intersects the plane $L_1: x-y+3z=6$ at the point $Q$. Another straight line which passes through $Q$ and is perpendicular to the plane $L_1$ intersects the plane $L_2: 2x-y+z=-4$ at the point $R$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The length of the line segment $PQ$ is $\sqrt6$
The centroid of the triangle $PQR$ is $\left(\frac43,\frac{14}{3},\frac53\right)$
The perimeter of the triangle $PQR$ is $\sqrt2+\sqrt6+\sqrt{11}$
questions.key_idea: Parameterise each line and substitute into the plane; then every statement is a coordinate computation.
solution: The line through $P(1,3,2)$ parallel to $(1,2,1)$ is $\vec r=(1,3,2)+\lambda(1,2,1)$.
It meets $L_1$ at $Q=(1+\lambda,3+2\lambda,2+\lambda)$: $(1+\lambda)-(3+2\lambda)+3(2+\lambda)=6$, so $4+2\lambda=6$ and $\lambda=1$.
The line through $Q$ perpendicular to $L_1$ has direction $(1,-1,3)$: $\vec r=(2,5,3)+\mu(1,-1,3)$, so $R=(2+\mu,5-\mu,3+3\mu)$.
(C) Centroid $=\left(\frac{1+2+1}{3},\frac{3+5+6}{3},\frac{2+3+0}{3}\right)=\left(\frac43,\frac{14}{3},\frac53\right)$. True.
(D) $QR=|(-1,1,-3)|=\sqrt{11}$ and $PR=|(0,3,-2)|=\sqrt{13}$, so the perimeter is $\sqrt6+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{13}\neq\sqrt2+\sqrt6+\sqrt{11}$. False. Answer (A), (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the ray-plane parameter formula $t=\frac{k-\vec n\cdot\vec p}{\vec n\cdot\vec d}$ and work with displacement vectors $\vec{PQ}$, $\vec{QR}$, getting $PR$ from their sum.
solution: $\vec n_1=(1,-1,3)$, $\vec n_2=(2,-1,1)$, $\vec d=(1,2,1)$. From $P$ along $\vec d$ to $L_1$: $t=\frac{6-\vec n_1\cdot P}{\vec n_1\cdot\vec d}=\frac{6-4}{2}=1$.
So $\vec{PQ}=\vec d=(1,2,1)$, $PQ=\sqrt6$ (A true) and $Q=(2,5,3)$.
From $Q$ along $\vec n_1$ to $L_2$: $t=\frac{-4-\vec n_2\cdot Q}{\vec n_2\cdot\vec n_1}=\frac{-4-2}{6}=-1$.
So $\vec{QR}=-\vec n_1=(-1,1,-3)$, $QR=\sqrt{11}$ and $R=Q-\vec n_1=(1,6,0)$: (B) false.
$\vec{PR}=\vec{PQ}+\vec{QR}=(0,3,-2)$, so $PR=\sqrt{13}$. Check: $PR^2=6+11+2(\vec{PQ}\cdot\vec{QR})=17+2(-2)=13$.
Perimeter $=\sqrt6+\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{13}$: (D) false.
Centroid $=P+\frac{\vec{PQ}+\vec{PR}}{3}=(1,3,2)+\frac{(1,5,-1)}{3}=\left(\frac43,\frac{14}{3},\frac53\right)$: (C) true. Answer (A), (C).

useful_results: A line $\vec p+t\vec d$ meets the plane $\vec n\cdot\vec x=k$ at $t=\frac{k-\vec n\cdot\vec p}{\vec n\cdot\vec d}$ (if $\vec n\cdot\vec d\neq0$). Here $t=1$ from $P$.
The line through a point perpendicular to the plane $ax+by+cz=k$ has direction $(a,b,c)$.
Distance along a direction from a point to a plane is (perpendicular distance)/(cosine of the angle with the normal): $PQ=\frac{2/\sqrt{11}}{2/\sqrt{66}}=\sqrt6$.
Centroid of a triangle is the mean of the vertices; always verify options against the computed coordinates (here $R=(1,6,0)$, not $(1,6,3)$).

concepts: Scalar triple product (coplanarity) and a point on a plane
questions.question: Let $\overrightarrow{OP}=\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\hat{i}+\frac{\beta-1}{\beta}\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\frac12\hat{k}$ be three vectors, where $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ and $O$ denotes the origin. If $\left(\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OQ}\right)\cdot\overrightarrow{OR}=0$ and the point $(\alpha,\beta,2)$ lies on the plane $3x+3y-z+l=0$, then the value of $l$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: A zero triple product means the determinant is $0$; it reduces to $\alpha+\beta+1=0$, and the plane needs only $\alpha+\beta$.
solution: $\left(\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OQ}\right)\cdot\overrightarrow{OR}$ is the scalar triple product, so the determinant of the three component rows must be $0$.
$\begin{vmatrix}\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}&1&1\\1&\frac{\beta-1}{\beta}&1\\1&1&\frac12\end{vmatrix}=0$.
Expand along the first row: $\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\left[\frac{\beta-1}{2\beta}-1\right]-1\left[\frac12-1\right]+1\left[1-\frac{\beta-1}{\beta}\right]=0$.
Simplify the brackets: $\frac{\beta-1}{2\beta}-1=-\frac{\beta+1}{2\beta}$ and $1-\frac{\beta-1}{\beta}=\frac1\beta$, so $-\frac{(\alpha-1)(\beta+1)}{2\alpha\beta}+\frac12+\frac1\beta=0$.
Multiply by $2\alpha\beta$: $-(\alpha-1)(\beta+1)+\alpha\beta+2\alpha=0$.
$-\alpha\beta-\alpha+\beta+1+\alpha\beta+2\alpha=0$, which gives $\alpha+\beta+1=0$.
The point $(\alpha,\beta,2)$ lies on $3x+3y-z+l=0$, so $3(\alpha+\beta)-2+l=0$.
Since $\alpha+\beta=-1$: $-3-2+l=0$, hence $l=5$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write each vector as $(1,1,1)$ minus a multiple of a basis vector and expand the triple product multilinearly.
solution: Put $a=\frac1\alpha$, $b=\frac1\beta$, $c=\frac12$ and $\vec s=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. Then $\overrightarrow{OP}=\vec s-a\hat{i}$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\vec s-b\hat{j}$, $\overrightarrow{OR}=\vec s-c\hat{k}$.
The triple product $[\vec s-a\hat{i},\ \vec s-b\hat{j},\ \vec s-c\hat{k}]$ is linear in each slot. Any term with $\vec s$ in two slots is $0$ (two equal vectors).
Terms with no $\vec s$: $[-a\hat{i},-b\hat{j},-c\hat{k}]=-abc$.
Terms with one $\vec s$: $bc[\vec s,\hat{j},\hat{k}]+ac[\hat{i},\vec s,\hat{k}]+ab[\hat{i},\hat{j},\vec s]=bc+ac+ab$, because each triple product picks one coordinate of $\vec s$, which is $1$.
So the condition is $ab+bc+ca-abc=0$.
With $c=\frac12$: $ab+\frac{a+b}{2}-\frac{ab}{2}=0$, i.e. $ab+a+b=0$.
Multiply by $\alpha\beta$: $1+\beta+\alpha=0$, so $\alpha+\beta=-1$.
Then $l=2-3(\alpha+\beta)=2+3=5$.

useful_results: Four points $O,P,Q,R$ are coplanar exactly when $\left[\overrightarrow{OP},\overrightarrow{OQ},\overrightarrow{OR}\right]=0$, i.e. the $3\times3$ determinant of components vanishes.

The triple product is linear in each slot and vanishes if two slots are equal or parallel. For $\vec s=(1,1,1)$: $[\vec s-a\hat{i},\vec s-b\hat{j},\vec s-c\hat{k}]=ab+bc+ca-abc$ (check $a,b,c=1,2,3$: both sides give $5$).
Entries like $\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}=1-\frac1\alpha$ signal substituting $a=\frac1\alpha$; the condition then becomes symmetric and simple.
When a later condition involves only a combination (here $\alpha+\beta$), solve for that combination rather than for each unknown.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and resolving a vector along $\vec a\times\vec b$
questions.question: Let $\vec p=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $\vec q=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. If for some real numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ we have $15\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+6\hat{k}=\alpha(2\vec p+\vec q)+\beta(\vec p-2\vec q)+\gamma(\vec p\times\vec q)$, then the value of $\gamma$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: $\vec p\times\vec q$ is perpendicular to $2\vec p+\vec q$ and $\vec p-2\vec q$, so dotting with it isolates $\gamma$.
solution: $\vec p\times\vec q$ is perpendicular to both $\vec p$ and $\vec q$, hence to $2\vec p+\vec q$ and $\vec p-2\vec q$.
Dot the given equation with $\vec p\times\vec q$: $(15\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+6\hat{k})\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)=\alpha\cdot0+\beta\cdot0+\gamma\left|\vec p\times\vec q\right|^2$.
$\vec p\times\vec q=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\2&1&3\\1&-1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat{i}(1+3)-\hat{j}(2-3)+\hat{k}(-2-1)=4\hat{i}+\hat{j}-3\hat{k}$.
$\left|\vec p\times\vec q\right|^2=16+1+9=26$.
So $52=26\gamma$, hence $\gamma=2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Compare components: the vector equation is three linear equations in $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, solved by elimination.
solution: $2\vec p+\vec q=(5,1,7)$, $\vec p-2\vec q=(0,3,1)$ and $\vec p\times\vec q=(4,1,-3)$.
Equating $x,y,z$ components: $5\alpha+4\gamma=15$, $\ \alpha+3\beta+\gamma=10$, $\ 7\alpha+\beta-3\gamma=6$.
From the second, $\beta=\frac{10-\alpha-\gamma}{3}$. Put this in the third: $21\alpha+10-\alpha-\gamma-9\gamma=18$, i.e. $10\alpha-5\gamma=4$.
From the first, $10\alpha=30-8\gamma$. Then $30-8\gamma-5\gamma=4$, so $13\gamma=26$ and $\gamma=2$.
Check: $\alpha=\frac75$, $\beta=\frac{11}{5}$ satisfy the second equation ($\frac75+\frac{33}{5}+2=10$) and the third ($\frac{49}{5}+\frac{11}{5}-6=6$).

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$ and $\vec b$, so dotting a vector equation with it kills every term lying in $\mathrm{span}(\vec a,\vec b)$ and leaves $\gamma=\frac{\vec v\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)}{|\vec a\times\vec b|^2}$ (for non-parallel $\vec a,\vec b$).
Lagrange identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$. Here $14\cdot3-4^2=26$.
$\vec a,\vec b,\vec a\times\vec b$ form a basis of space whenever $\vec a\nparallel\vec b$, so the coefficients $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are unique.
Triple-product (Cramer) form: if $\vec v=\alpha\vec a'+\beta\vec b'+\gamma\vec c'$ then $\gamma=\frac{[\vec v,\vec a',\vec b']}{[\vec c',\vec a',\vec b']}$.

concepts: Coplanar lines, point of intersection and unit normal to a plane
questions.question:
Let $\gamma\in\mathbb{R}$ be such that the lines $L_1:\frac{x+11}{1}=\frac{y+21}{2}=\frac{z+29}{3}$ and $L_2:\frac{x+16}{3}=\frac{y+11}{2}=\frac{z+4}{\gamma}$ intersect. Let $R_1$ be the point of intersection of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Let $O=(0,0,0)$, and $\hat n$ denote a unit normal vector to the plane containing both the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$. Match each entry in List-I to the correct entry in List-II.
List-I: (P) $\gamma$ equals; (Q) A possible choice for $\hat n$ is; (R) $\overrightarrow{OR_1}$ equals; (S) A possible value of $\overrightarrow{OR_1}\cdot\hat n$ is.
List-II: (1) $-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$; (2) $\sqrt{\frac32}$; (3) $1$; (4) $\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\hat{i}-\frac{2}{\sqrt6}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\hat{k}$; (5) $\sqrt{\frac23}$.
questions.key_idea: Intersecting lines are coplanar, so a $3\times3$ determinant gives $\gamma$; the normal is the cross product of the directions.
solution: (P) Intersecting lines are coplanar: $\begin{vmatrix}x_2-x_1&y_2-y_1&z_2-z_1\\a_1&b_1&c_1\\a_2&b_2&c_2\end{vmatrix}=0$ (a sign flip of the first row does not change the condition).
(Q) Direction vectors are $\vec p=(1,2,3)$ and $\vec q=(3,2,1)$. A normal is $\vec n=\vec p\times\vec q=(2-6,\ 9-1,\ 2-6)=-4\hat{i}+8\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$.
$|\vec n|=\sqrt{16+64+16}=4\sqrt6$, so a unit normal is $\hat n=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\hat{i}-\frac{2}{\sqrt6}\hat{j}+\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\hat{k}$. (Q) $\to$ (4).
(R) Point of intersection: $(\lambda-11,\ 2\lambda-21,\ 3\lambda-29)=(3\mu-16,\ 2\mu-11,\ \mu-4)$.
Compare $x$ and $y$: $\lambda-11=3\mu-16$ and $2\lambda-21=2\mu-11$. The second gives $\lambda=\mu+5$; then $\mu-6=3\mu-16$, so $\mu=5$, $\lambda=10$ (the $z$ values agree: $1=1$).
$R_1=(-1,-1,1)$, so $\overrightarrow{OR_1}=-\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$. (R) $\to$ (1).
(S) $\overrightarrow{OR_1}\cdot\hat n=(-1,-1,1)\cdot\frac{(1,-2,1)}{\sqrt6}=\frac{-1+2+1}{\sqrt6}=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\frac23}$. (S) $\to$ (5).
So (P) $\to$ (3), (Q) $\to$ (4), (R) $\to$ (1), (S) $\to$ (5), which is option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $R_1$ from two coordinates first, then $\gamma$ from the third; find $\hat n$ from sum and difference of the directions.
solution: Use only the $x$ and $y$ equations (no $\gamma$ needed): $\lambda-11=3\mu-16$ and $2\lambda-21=2\mu-11$ give $\lambda=10$, $\mu=5$. From $L_1$, $R_1=(-1,-1,1)$, so (R) $\to$ (1).
$R_1$ lies on $L_2$, so $\frac{z+4}{\gamma}=\mu$ with $z=1$: $5=5\gamma$, hence $\gamma=1$. (P) $\to$ (3).
A normal $\vec n$ is perpendicular to $(1,2,3)$ and $(3,2,1)$. Adding: $\vec n\cdot(4,4,4)=0$, so $n_1+n_2+n_3=0$. Subtracting: $\vec n\cdot(2,0,-2)=0$, so $n_1=n_3$.
Hence $\vec n\propto(1,-2,1)$ and $\hat n=\pm\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,-2,1)$; the $+$ sign is option (4). (Q) $\to$ (4).
The plane is $x-2y+z=d$; $R_1$ lies on it, so $d=-1+2+1=2$.
For any point $R_1$ of the plane, $\overrightarrow{OR_1}\cdot\hat n=\frac{d}{\sqrt6}=\frac{2}{\sqrt6}=\sqrt{\frac23}$, the distance of the plane from $O$. (S) $\to$ (5).

useful_results: Lines $\vec a_1+\lambda\vec d_1$ and $\vec a_2+\mu\vec d_2$ are coplanar iff $[\vec a_2-\vec a_1,\vec d_1,\vec d_2]=0$; they intersect iff coplanar and $\vec d_1\nparallel\vec d_2$.

A unit normal to the plane of the two lines is $\pm\frac{\vec d_1\times\vec d_2}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$; both signs are valid choices. For directions $(a,b,c)$ and $(c,b,a)$ the cross product is $(a-c)(b,-(a+c),b)$ (here $(-2)(2,-4,2)$).
If $R$ is any point of a plane and $\hat n$ a unit normal, then $\overrightarrow{OR}\cdot\hat n=\pm$ (distance of the plane from $O$), the same for every point of the plane.
To intersect two lines, equate two coordinates to find the parameters and use the third as a check (or as the equation for an unknown constant).

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Line of intersection of planes, foot of perpendicular and distance from a plane
questions.question: Let $L_1$ be the line of intersection of the planes given by the equations $2x+3y+z=4$ and $x+2y+z=5$. Let $L_2$ be the line passing through the point $P(2,-1,3)$ and parallel to $L_1$. Let $M$ denote the plane given by the equation $2x+y-2z=6$. Suppose that the line $L_2$ meets the plane $M$ at the point $Q$. Let $R$ be the foot of perpendicular drawn from $P$ to the plane $M$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The length of the line segment $PQ$ is $9\sqrt3$
The length of the line segment $QR$ is $15$
The acute angle between the line segments $PQ$ and $PR$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}\right)$
questions.key_idea: $PR\perp M$ makes $\triangle PRQ$ right-angled at $R$, so $PQ$ and $PR$ give $QR$, the area and the angle.
solution: Direction of $L_1$ is the cross product of the normals: $\vec d=(2,3,1)\times(1,2,1)=\hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}$.
$L_2$ passes through $P(2,-1,3)$ with direction $(1,-1,1)$: $Q=(2+\lambda,\,-1-\lambda,\,3+\lambda)$.
$Q$ lies on $M$: $2(2+\lambda)+(-1-\lambda)-2(3+\lambda)=6$, i.e. $-3-\lambda=6$, so $\lambda=-9$ and $Q=(-7,8,-6)$.
$PR\perp M$, so $PR$ is along the normal $(2,1,-2)$: $R=(2+2\mu,\,-1+\mu,\,3-2\mu)$.
$PQ=|\lambda|\sqrt3=9\sqrt3$ and $PR=\left|(2,1,-2)\right|=3$.
$PR$ is perpendicular to the plane $M$, which contains $Q$ and $R$, so $PR\perp QR$: $\triangle PQR$ is right-angled at $R$ and $QR=\sqrt{PQ^2-PR^2}=\sqrt{243-9}=\sqrt{234}$.
(A) $PQ=9\sqrt3$: true. (B) $QR=\sqrt{234}\approx15.3\neq15$: false.
(C) Area $=\frac12\,QR\cdot PR=\frac12\sqrt{234}\cdot3=\frac32\sqrt{234}$: true.
(D) $\cos\theta=\frac{PR}{PQ}=\frac{3}{9\sqrt3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}\neq\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}$: false. So the answer is (A, C).
questions.correction_note: The PDF substitutes Q into the plane as 2(2+lambda)+(-1-lambda)-2(3+2lambda)=6; the z-coordinate of Q is 3+lambda, not 3+2lambda (the printed equation would give lambda=-3). With 3+lambda one gets lambda=-9, Q(-7,8,-6) as the PDF uses. The PDF also states no verdicts for (B) and (D) and does not justify the right angle at R; these are filled in.

alternate_solutions.idea: No coordinates of $Q,R$: use $PR$ = distance of $P$ from $M$ and the angle between $L_2$ and the normal of $M$ in the right triangle $PRQ$.
solution: $L_1$ has direction $\vec d=(2,3,1)\times(1,2,1)=(1,-1,1)$; the normal of $M$ is $\vec n=(2,1,-2)$ with $|\vec n|=3$.
$PR$ is the distance of $P(2,-1,3)$ from $M$: $PR=\frac{|2\cdot2-1-2\cdot3-6|}{3}=\frac{9}{3}=3$.

$\triangle PRQ$ is right-angled at $R$. The angle $\theta$ at $P$ is the angle between $L_2$ (direction $\vec d$) and the normal: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}=\frac{|2-1-2|}{\sqrt3\cdot3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}$.
$PQ=\frac{PR}{\cos\theta}=3\cdot3\sqrt3=9\sqrt3$. (A) true.
$\cos^2\theta=\frac{1}{27}$, so $\tan^2\theta=\frac{26/27}{1/27}=26$ and $QR=PR\tan\theta=3\sqrt{26}=\sqrt{234}\approx15.3$. (B) false.
Area $=\frac12\,PR\cdot QR=\frac12\cdot3\cdot3\sqrt{26}=\frac92\sqrt{26}=\frac32\sqrt{234}$. (C) true.
The angle between $PQ$ and $PR$ is $\theta$ with $\cos\theta=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}$, not $\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}$. (D) false. Answer (A, C).

useful_results: The line of intersection of planes with normals $\vec n_1,\vec n_2$ has direction $\vec n_1\times\vec n_2$.
Distance of $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from $Ax+By+Cz+D=0$ is $\frac{|Ax_0+By_0+Cz_0+D|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2+C^2}}$, and the foot is $P-\frac{Ax_0+By_0+Cz_0+D}{A^2+B^2+C^2}(A,B,C)$.

If a line through $P$ meets a plane at $Q$ and $R$ is the foot from $P$, then $\triangle PRQ$ is right-angled at $R$ with $PQ=\frac{PR}{|\cos\varphi|}$ and $QR=PR\tan\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the angle between the line and the normal.
The angle between a line (direction $\vec d$) and a plane (normal $\vec n$) is $\alpha$ with $\sin\alpha=\frac{|\vec d\cdot\vec n|}{|\vec d||\vec n|}$; it equals $90^\circ-\varphi$.

concepts: Position vectors: section formula, weighted centroid and midpoints
questions.question: For any two points $M$ and $N$ in the $XY$-plane, let $\overrightarrow{MN}$ denote the vector from $M$ to $N$, and $\vec 0$ denote the zero vector. Let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be three distinct points in the $XY$-plane. Let $S$ be a point inside the triangle $\triangle PQR$ such that $\overrightarrow{SP}+5\overrightarrow{SQ}+6\overrightarrow{SR}=\vec 0$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the mid-points of the sides $PR$ and $QR$, respectively. Then the value of $\frac{\text{length of the line segment }EF}{\text{length of the line segment }ES}$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: With $P$ as origin, $S=\frac{5\vec q+6\vec r}{12}$, so $\overrightarrow{ES}$ and $\overrightarrow{EF}$ are both multiples of $\vec q$.
solution: Take $P$ as the origin and let $\vec q,\vec r,\vec x$ be the position vectors of $Q,R,S$. Then $\overrightarrow{SP}=-\vec x$, $\overrightarrow{SQ}=\vec q-\vec x$, $\overrightarrow{SR}=\vec r-\vec x$.
The condition becomes $-\vec x+5(\vec q-\vec x)+6(\vec r-\vec x)=\vec 0$.
So $12\vec x=5\vec q+6\vec r$, i.e. $\vec x=\frac{5\vec q+6\vec r}{12}$.
$E$ is the midpoint of $PR$: $\vec e=\frac{\vec r}{2}$. $F$ is the midpoint of $QR$: $\vec f=\frac{\vec q+\vec r}{2}$.
$\overrightarrow{EF}=\vec f-\vec e=\frac{\vec q}{2}$.
$\overrightarrow{ES}=\vec x-\vec e=\frac{5\vec q+6\vec r}{12}-\frac{6\vec r}{12}=\frac{5\vec q}{12}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The answer is claimed to be the same for every such triangle, so compute it for one convenient triangle in coordinates.
solution: The problem asks for a single number, so it does not depend on the triangle. Choose $P=(0,0)$, $Q=(2,0)$, $R=(0,2)$.
$S$ is inside the triangle: $x>0$, $y>0$ and $x+y=\frac{11}{6}<2$.
$EF=1$ and $ES=\frac56-0=\frac56$ (both segments lie on $y=1$).

useful_results: $\sum w_i\overrightarrow{SA_i}=\vec 0$ means $S=\frac{\sum w_iA_i}{\sum w_i}$ (weights summing to a non-zero value); $S$ is inside the triangle iff all weights have the same sign.
Midpoint theorem: the segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length, so $EF=\frac12PQ$.

With weights $w_P,w_Q,w_R$ (total $W$) and $E$ the midpoint of $PR$: $\overrightarrow{ES}=\frac{w_Q}{W}\overrightarrow{PQ}+\left(\frac{w_R}{W}-\frac12\right)\overrightarrow{PR}$. When $w_R=\frac W2$ (here $6$ of $12$), $S$ lies on the line through $E$ parallel to $PQ$.
When a problem promises a unique numerical value for any triangle, test one convenient coordinate triangle.

concepts: Coplanarity of vectors (scalar triple product)
Determinants (circulant determinant)
questions.question: Consider the vectors $\vec x=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $\vec y=2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, and $\vec z=3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. For two distinct positive real numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$, define $\vec X=\alpha\vec x+\beta\vec y-\vec z$, $\vec Y=\alpha\vec y+\beta\vec z-\vec x$, and $\vec Z=\alpha\vec z+\beta\vec x-\vec y$. If the vectors $\vec X,\vec Y$ and $\vec Z$ lie in a plane, then the value of $\alpha+\beta-3$ is ______.
questions.key_idea: Coplanarity needs the coefficient determinant to vanish; it factors as $(\alpha+\beta-1)$ times a factor that is never $0$ for positive $\alpha,\beta$.
solution: Write $\vec X,\vec Y,\vec Z$ in terms of $\vec x,\vec y,\vec z$: the coefficient rows are $(\alpha,\beta,-1)$, $(-1,\alpha,\beta)$, $(\beta,-1,\alpha)$. So $[\vec X\,\vec Y\,\vec Z]=\Delta\,[\vec x\,\vec y\,\vec z]$, where $\Delta$ is the determinant of these rows.
$\vec X,\vec Y,\vec Z$ coplanar means $[\vec X\,\vec Y\,\vec Z]=0$, hence $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&\beta&-1\\-1&\alpha&\beta\\\beta&-1&\alpha\end{vmatrix}=0$.
Apply $R_1\to R_1+R_2+R_3$: the first row becomes $(\alpha+\beta-1)(1,1,1)$, so $\Delta=(\alpha+\beta-1)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\-1&\alpha&\beta\\\beta&-1&\alpha\end{vmatrix}=0$.
Expand the $3\times3$ determinant: $1(\alpha^2+\beta)-1(-\alpha-\beta^2)+1(1-\alpha\beta)=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\alpha+\beta+1-\alpha\beta$.
So $(\alpha+\beta-1)\left(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\alpha+\beta+1-\alpha\beta\right)=0$, i.e. $\alpha+\beta=1$ or $\alpha^2+(1-\beta)\alpha+\beta^2+\beta+1=0$.
Treat the second as a quadratic in $\alpha$: discriminant $(1-\beta)^2-4(\beta^2+\beta+1)=-3\beta^2-6\beta-3=-3(\beta+1)^2$.
For real $\alpha$ we need $D\ge0$, so $(\beta+1)^2\le0$, i.e. $\beta=-1$, which is not possible as $\beta>0$.
Hence $\alpha+\beta=1$ and $\alpha+\beta-3=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The coefficient matrix is circulant, so $\Delta=a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc$ with $(a,b,c)=(\alpha,\beta,-1)$, a product with a sum of squares.
solution: The rows $(\alpha,\beta,-1)$, $(-1,\alpha,\beta)$, $(\beta,-1,\alpha)$ have the form $(a,b,c)$, $(c,a,b)$, $(b,c,a)$ with $a=\alpha$, $b=\beta$, $c=-1$: a circulant.
Its determinant is $a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)\cdot\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]$.
Since $[\vec x\,\vec y\,\vec z]=-18\neq0$, the vectors $\vec X,\vec Y,\vec Z$ are coplanar iff this determinant is $0$.
So $a+b+c=0$ (i.e. $\alpha+\beta=1$) or $a=b=c$ (i.e. $\alpha=\beta=-1$).
The second case contradicts $\alpha,\beta>0$, so $\alpha+\beta=1$.
Direct check: $\vec X+\vec Y+\vec Z=(\alpha+\beta-1)(\vec x+\vec y+\vec z)=\vec 0$ when $\alpha+\beta=1$, so the three vectors are dependent and coplanar.
Therefore $\alpha+\beta-3=-2$.

useful_results: If $\vec x,\vec y,\vec z$ are non-coplanar and $\vec X,\vec Y,\vec Z$ have coefficient matrix $C$ in this basis, then $[\vec X\,\vec Y\,\vec Z]=\det C\,[\vec x\,\vec y\,\vec z]$. So coplanarity of the new vectors is just $\det C=0$.
Circulant $3\times3$: $\begin{vmatrix}a&b&c\\c&a&b\\b&c&a\end{vmatrix}=a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)\left(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca\right)$. The second factor is $\frac12\sum(a-b)^2\ge0$, zero only if $a=b=c$.
If $\vec X+\vec Y+\vec Z=\vec 0$ (or any linear relation) the three vectors are linearly dependent, hence coplanar.
Row operation $R_1\to R_1+R_2+R_3$ makes a common factor appear in cyclic determinants; check by testing $(a,b,c)=(1,2,3)$: $\Delta=36-18=18$, and $6\cdot\frac12(1+1+4)=18$.

Homogeneous system of linear equations
questions.question:
Let $\vec w=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$, and $\vec u$ and $\vec v$ be two vectors, such that $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec w$ and $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u$. Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$, and $t$ be real numbers such that $\vec u=\alpha\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$, $-t\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$, $\alpha-t\beta+\gamma=0$, and $\alpha+\beta-t\gamma=0$. Match each entry in List-I to the correct entry in List-II and choose the correct option.
List-I: (P) $|\vec v|^2$ is equal to; (Q) If $\alpha=\sqrt3$, then $\gamma^2$ is equal to; (R) If $\alpha=\sqrt3$, then $(\beta+\gamma)^2$ is equal to; (S) If $\alpha=\sqrt2$, then $t+3$ is equal to.
List-II: (1) $0$; (2) $1$; (3) $2$; (4) $3$; (5) $5$.
questions.key_idea: $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are mutually perpendicular, and subtracting the equations gives $(1+t)(\alpha-\beta)=(1+t)(\beta-\gamma)=0$.
solution: $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec w$ gives $\vec w\perp\vec u,\vec v$; $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u$ gives $\vec u\perp\vec v,\vec w$. So $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are mutually perpendicular (all non-zero).
(P) $(\vec v\times\vec w)\times\vec v=(\vec v\cdot\vec v)\vec w-(\vec w\cdot\vec v)\vec v$, and the left side equals $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec w$.
So $\left(|\vec v|^2-1\right)\vec w-(\vec w\cdot\vec v)\vec v=\vec 0$. As $\vec w\perp\vec v$, $\vec w\cdot\vec v=0$ and $\vec w\neq\vec 0$, hence $|\vec v|^2=1$. (P) $\to$ (2).
From $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u$ with $\vec v\perp\vec w$: $|\vec u|=|\vec v||\vec w|=1\cdot\sqrt{1+1+4}=\sqrt6$.
Also $\vec u\cdot\vec w=0$ gives $\alpha+\beta-2\gamma=0$.
Subtract the equations: (ii)$-$(i) gives $\alpha(1+t)-\beta(1+t)=0$; (iii)$-$(ii) gives $\beta(1+t)-\gamma(1+t)=0$.
So $(1+t)(\alpha-\beta)=(1+t)(\beta-\gamma)=0$: either $t=-1$ or $\alpha=\beta=\gamma$.
(S) If $\alpha=\beta=\gamma$: $|\vec u|^2=3\alpha^2=6$, so $\alpha=\pm\sqrt2$; equation (i) gives $-t\alpha+2\alpha=0$, so $t=2$. For $\alpha=\sqrt2$: $t+3=5$. (S) $\to$ (5).
(Q) $\alpha=\sqrt3$ is not $\pm\sqrt2$, so this is the case $t=-1$, and every equation becomes $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$.
Combine with $\alpha+\beta-2\gamma=0$: subtracting gives $3\gamma=0$, so $\gamma=0$ and $\gamma^2=0$. (Q) $\to$ (1).
(R) Then $\beta=-\alpha$, so $(\beta+\gamma)^2=\beta^2=\alpha^2=3$. (R) $\to$ (4).
questions.correction_note: The PDF concludes alpha = 0 from alpha+beta+gamma = 0 and alpha+beta-2gamma = 0; subtracting gives gamma = 0 (alpha is not 0, it is sqrt(3)); the PDF then uses gamma^2 = 0 for (Q), so the final mapping is unaffected. It also prints a stray 8 in equation (1) and omits the justification for t = -1 when alpha = sqrt(3). Corrected and filled in.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rewrite each equation as $S=(t+1)\alpha$ with $S=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$, and use $|\vec w|=|\vec u||\vec v|$ for the lengths and a cross product for $\vec u$.
solution: Lengths: $\vec u\perp\vec v$ and $\vec v\perp\vec w$, so $|\vec w|=|\vec u||\vec v|$ and $|\vec u|=|\vec v||\vec w|$. Then $|\vec u|=|\vec v|^2|\vec u|$, so $|\vec v|^2=1$ (P) $\to$ (2), and $|\vec u|=|\vec w|=\sqrt6$.
Let $S=\alpha+\beta+\gamma$. Equation (i) is $S-(t+1)\alpha=0$; likewise (ii) is $S=(t+1)\beta$ and (iii) is $S=(t+1)\gamma$.
If $t\neq-1$: $\alpha=\beta=\gamma=\frac{S}{t+1}$, so $|\vec u|^2=3\alpha^2=6$ gives $\alpha=\pm\sqrt2$, and $S=3\alpha=(t+1)\alpha$ gives $t=2$. For $\alpha=\sqrt2$: $t+3=5$. (S) $\to$ (5).
If $t=-1$: $S=0$, i.e. $\vec u\perp(1,1,1)$. Also $\vec u\perp\vec w=(1,1,-2)$. So $\vec u\parallel(1,1,1)\times(1,1,-2)=(-3,3,0)$.
Hence $\vec u=k(1,-1,0)$ with $2k^2=6$, so $k=\pm\sqrt3$. With $\alpha=\sqrt3$: $\vec u=(\sqrt3,-\sqrt3,0)$, giving $\gamma^2=0$ (Q) $\to$ (1) and $(\beta+\gamma)^2=3$ (R) $\to$ (4).
Check: $\alpha=\sqrt3$ cannot come from the case $t\neq-1$ (it needs $\alpha=\pm\sqrt2$), so $t=-1$ is forced.

useful_results: If $\vec u\times\vec v=\vec w$ and $\vec v\times\vec w=\vec u$ with non-zero vectors, then $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are mutually perpendicular, $|\vec v|=1$, $|\vec u|=|\vec w|$ and $\vec w\times\vec u=\vec v$ also holds.

Triple-product identities: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec b\cdot\vec c)\vec a$ and $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$. For perpendicular $\vec a,\vec b$: $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|$.

The system $-t\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\alpha-t\beta+\gamma=\alpha+\beta-t\gamma=0$ has the matrix $J-(t+1)I$ ($J$ all ones), with determinant $-(t-2)(t+1)^2$. Non-zero solutions: $t=2$ with $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\propto(1,1,1)$, or $t=-1$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0$.
Writing symmetric equations as $S=(t+1)\alpha$, $S=(t+1)\beta$, $S=(t+1)\gamma$ splits cases immediately: either $t=-1$ or all unknowns are equal.

concepts: Dot and cross product: area of a triangle
questions.question: Let $\vec a,\vec b$ be two vectors, and let $P$, $Q$ and $R$ be the points with position vectors $\vec a$, $\vec b$ and $\vec a+\vec b$, respectively, with respect to the origin $O$. If $|\vec a+\vec b|=\sqrt{21}$, $|\vec a-\vec b|=3$, and $\vec a$ and $(\vec a-\vec b)$ are perpendicular to each other, then the area of the triangle $OPR$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\perp(\vec a-\vec b)$ gives $|\vec a|^2=\vec a\cdot\vec b$, and $\vec a\times(\vec a+\vec b)=\vec a\times\vec b$ gives area $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$.
solution: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2+2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=21$ and $|\vec a-\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2-2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=9$.
Adding: $|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2=15$. Subtracting: $4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b=12$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$.
$\vec a\perp(\vec a-\vec b)$ gives $\vec a\cdot(\vec a-\vec b)=0$, so $|\vec a|^2=\vec a\cdot\vec b=3$. Then $|\vec b|^2=15-3=12$.
Area of $\triangle OPR=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OR}\right|=\frac12\left|\vec a\times(\vec a+\vec b)\right|=\frac12\left|\vec a\times\vec b\right|$.
$|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}=\sqrt{36-9}=3\sqrt3$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot3\sqrt3=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. Option (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Geometry: $\vec a\perp(\vec a-\vec b)$ means $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$; $OPRQ$ is a parallelogram, so $[OPR]=[OPQ]$.
solution: $OPRQ$ is a parallelogram ($\vec{OR}=\vec{OP}+\vec{OQ}$) with diagonals $OR=\sqrt{21}$ and $PQ=|\vec a-\vec b|=3$.
The diagonal $OR$ splits it into two equal triangles, but so does $PQ$: $[OPR]=[OPQ]=\frac12[OPRQ]$.
$\vec{PQ}=\vec b-\vec a$ is perpendicular to $\vec a=\vec{OP}$, so $\triangle OPQ$ is right-angled at $P$ and $OQ^2=OP^2+PQ^2=OP^2+9$.
Parallelogram law: $OR^2+PQ^2=2(OP^2+OQ^2)$, so $21+9=2\left(OP^2+OP^2+9\right)$, giving $OP^2=3$.
$[OPQ]=\frac12\cdot OP\cdot PQ=\frac12\cdot\sqrt3\cdot3=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$, so $[OPR]=\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$. Option (C).

useful_results: Parallelogram law: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2\left(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2\right)$, and $|\vec a+\vec b|^2-|\vec a-\vec b|^2=4\,\vec a\cdot\vec b$.

For vertices $O,\vec a,\vec c$: area $=\frac12|\vec a\times\vec c|$. With $\vec c=\vec a+\vec b$ the $\vec a\times\vec a$ term vanishes, so $[O,\vec a,\vec a+\vec b]=[O,\vec a,\vec b]$ (half the parallelogram).
Lagrange: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ (here $36-9=27$).
$\vec a\perp(\vec a-\vec b)\iff|\vec a|^2=\vec a\cdot\vec b$, i.e. $\vec b$ projects onto $\vec a$ with length $|\vec a|$: right angle at $P$ in $\triangle OPQ$.

concepts: Plane through a line perpendicular to a given plane; distance and angle between planes
questions.question: Let $P$ be the plane such that it contains the straight line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$ and is perpendicular to the plane $x+2y+3z=4$. Let $P_1$ be the plane which passes through the point $(4,2,2)$ and is parallel to $P$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
options: The equation of the plane $P$ is $7x-5y+z=-10$
The distance between the planes $P$ and $P_1$ is $30$
The distance of the plane $P$ from the origin is $2\sqrt3$
The acute angle between the plane $P$ and the plane $2x+2y+z=3$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}\right)$
questions.key_idea: The normal of $P$ is $\vec d\times\vec n_Q$: perpendicular to the line direction and to the normal of the given plane.
solution: The line has direction $\vec d=(2,3,1)$ and lies in $P$, so the normal $\vec n_P\perp\vec d$.
$P$ is perpendicular to $x+2y+3z=4$ (normal $\vec n_Q=(1,2,3)$), so $\vec n_P\perp\vec n_Q$.
$\vec n_P=\vec d\times\vec n_Q=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\2&3&1\\1&2&3\end{vmatrix}=7\hat{i}-5\hat{j}+\hat{k}$.
(B) Distance between the parallel planes $=\frac{|10-(-20)|}{\sqrt{49+25+1}}=\frac{30}{\sqrt{75}}=\frac{30}{5\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3\neq30$. False.
(C) Distance of $P$ from the origin $=\frac{|10|}{\sqrt{75}}=\frac{10}{5\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\neq2\sqrt3$. False.
(D) $\cos\theta=\frac{|(7,-5,1)\cdot(2,2,1)|}{\sqrt{75}\cdot3}=\frac{5}{5\sqrt3\cdot3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}$, so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}\right)$. True.
Answer: (A, D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write the line as an intersection of two planes and use the pencil of planes through it, imposing perpendicularity on the normals.
solution: From $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-3}{3}$: $3x-2y+3=0$. From $\frac{y-3}{3}=\frac{z+2}{1}$: $y-3z-9=0$. The line is their intersection.
Every plane through the line: $(3x-2y+3)+\lambda(y-3z-9)=0$, with normal $(3,\ \lambda-2,\ -3\lambda)$.
Perpendicular to $x+2y+3z=4$: $3+2(\lambda-2)-9\lambda=0$, so $-1-7\lambda=0$ and $\lambda=-\frac17$.
Substitute and multiply by $7$: $21x-15y+3z+30=0$, i.e. $7x-5y+z+10=0$. (A) true.
Value of $7x-5y+z+10$ at $(4,2,2)$ is $28-10+2+10=30$; distance from $P$ to $P_1$ is $\frac{30}{\sqrt{75}}=2\sqrt3\neq30$. (B) false.
Distance of $P$ from $O$ is $\frac{10}{\sqrt{75}}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}\neq2\sqrt3$. (C) false.
Angle between normals $(7,-5,1)$ and $(2,2,1)$: $\cos\theta=\frac{5}{\sqrt{75}\cdot3}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt3}$. (D) true. Answer (A, D).

useful_results: A plane containing a line of direction $\vec d$ and perpendicular to a plane with normal $\vec m$ has normal $\vec d\times\vec m$ (it must be perpendicular to both).
Pencil of planes: planes through the intersection of $\pi_1=0$ and $\pi_2=0$ are $\pi_1+\lambda\pi_2=0$; a symmetric-form line is the intersection of two of its three equalities.
Parallel planes $Ax+By+Cz+D_1=0$ and $Ax+By+Cz+D_2=0$ are at distance $\frac{|D_1-D_2|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2+C^2}}$; this is also (value of one plane's expression at a point of the other)$/|\vec n|$.
Angle between planes: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2|}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_2|}$ (acute angle). Always sanity-check: $\vec d\cdot\vec n_P=14-15+1=0$ and $(1,3,-2)$ satisfies the plane.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular, section formula, area and orthocentre of a triangle in 3D
questions.question: Let $L$ be the straight line joining the points $P(1,2,-1)$ and $Q(2,3,1)$. Let $S$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $R(4,-1,5)$ to the line $L$. Another line passing through $R$ intersects $L$ at a point $T$ such that the point $S$ divides the line segment $PT$ internally in the ratio $|PS|:|ST|=1:2$, where $|PS|$ and $|ST|$ are the lengths of the line segments $PS$ and $ST$, respectively. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE:
options: The orthocentre of the triangle $PRT$ is $\left(\frac{23}{5},-4,\frac{31}{5}\right)$
The orthocentre of the triangle $PRT$ is $(4,3,5)$
The area of the triangle $PRT$ is $6\sqrt5$
The area of the triangle $PRT$ is $18\sqrt5$
questions.key_idea: $RS\perp PT$ makes $RS$ the altitude on $PT$, so $H$ lies on line $RS$ and area is a base-height product.
solution: Line $L$ through $P(1,2,-1)$ with direction $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(1,1,2)$: $S=(1+\lambda,\ 2+\lambda,\ -1+2\lambda)$.
$\overrightarrow{RS}=(\lambda-3,\ \lambda+3,\ 2\lambda-6)$ and $\overrightarrow{RS}\cdot(1,1,2)=0$: $(\lambda-3)+(\lambda+3)+2(2\lambda-6)=0$, so $6\lambda-12=0$ and $\lambda=2$.
$S$ divides $PT$ internally in $1:2$, so $S=\frac{2P+T}{3}$. With $T=(x,y,z)$: $\frac{2+x}{3}=3\Rightarrow x=7$; $\frac{4+y}{3}=4\Rightarrow y=8$; $\frac{-2+z}{3}=3\Rightarrow z=11$. $T=(7,8,11)$.

$\overrightarrow{PR}=(3,-3,6)$ and $\overrightarrow{RT}=(3,9,6)$; $\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{RT}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\3&-3&6\\3&9&6\end{vmatrix}=-72\hat{i}+36\hat{k}=36(-2\hat{i}+\hat{k})$.
Area of $\triangle PRT=\frac12\left|\overrightarrow{PR}\times\overrightarrow{RT}\right|=\frac12\cdot36\sqrt5=18\sqrt5$. (D) true, (C) false.
Orthocentre: $RS\perp PT$ (as $PT$ lies on $L$), so the altitude from $R$ is the line $RS$ and $H$ lies on it. With $\overrightarrow{RS}=(-1,5,-2)$: $H=(4-\mu,\ -1+5\mu,\ 5-2\mu)$.
The altitude from $P$ is perpendicular to $RT$: $\overrightarrow{PH}\cdot\overrightarrow{RT}=0$ with $\overrightarrow{PH}=(3-\mu,\ -3+5\mu,\ 6-2\mu)$.
$H=\left(4+\frac35,\ -1-3,\ 5+\frac65\right)=\left(\frac{23}{5},-4,\frac{31}{5}\right)$. (A) true, (B) false. Answer (A, D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use base and height ($PT$, $RS$) for the area, and place the triangle in plane coordinates with $S$ as origin to get $H$ from $SH\cdot SR=SP\cdot ST$.
solution: Foot of perpendicular by projection: $\overrightarrow{PR}=(3,-3,6)$, $\vec d=(1,1,2)$, $\frac{\overrightarrow{PR}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}=\frac{12}{6}=2$, so $S=P+2\vec d=(3,4,3)$; and $T=3S-2P=(7,8,11)$.
$RS\perp PT$, so area $=\frac12\cdot PT\cdot RS=\frac12\cdot6\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt{30}=3\sqrt{180}=18\sqrt5$. (D) true, (C) false.
In the plane of the triangle take $S$ as origin and $PT$ as the $x$-axis: $P=(-2\sqrt6,0)$, $T=(4\sqrt6,0)$, $R=(0,\sqrt{30})$. $H$ lies on the altitude $RS$, so $H=(0,y)$.
$\overrightarrow{PH}\cdot\overrightarrow{RT}=0$: $(2\sqrt6,\ y)\cdot(4\sqrt6,\ -\sqrt{30})=48-\sqrt{30}\,y=0$, so $y=\frac{48}{\sqrt{30}}$.

$\frac{SH}{SR}=\frac{48/\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{30}}=\frac{48}{30}=\frac85$, with $H$ on the same side of $S$ as $R$ (beyond $R$, as the angle at $R$ is obtuse: $\overrightarrow{RP}\cdot\overrightarrow{RT}=-18<0$).
$H=S+\frac85(R-S)=(3,4,3)+\frac85(1,-5,2)=\left(\frac{23}{5},-4,\frac{31}{5}\right)$. (A) true, (B) false. Answer (A, D).

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line through $P$ with direction $\vec d$: $S=P+\frac{(R-P)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$.
If $S$ divides $PT$ internally in $m:n$ ($PS:ST=m:n$), then $T=\frac{(m+n)S-nP}{m}$; for $1:2$, $T=3S-2P$.

Orthocentre with altitude foot $S$ on base $PT$: in coordinates $P=(-p,0)$, $T=(t,0)$, $R=(0,r)$ ($p,t,r>0$) the orthocentre is $(0,\frac{pt}{r})$, i.e. $SH\cdot SR=SP\cdot ST$ with $H$ on the ray $SR$. It lies outside the triangle exactly when $pt>r^2$ (angle at $R$ obtuse); here $48>30$.
Triangle area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$, or $\frac12\cdot$base$\cdot$height when a foot of the altitude is known.

concepts: Orthogonal matrix ($MM^T=I$)
Triple product and cross product of orthonormal vectors
questions.question:
For real numbers $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ and $\mu$, consider the $3\times3$ matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\frac{1}{\sqrt2}&-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\\\frac{1}{\sqrt3}&\beta&\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\\\gamma&\delta&\mu\end{pmatrix}$. Suppose that $MM^T=I$, where $M^T$ is the transpose of the matrix $M$, and $I$ is the $3\times3$ identity matrix. Let the three column vectors be defined as $\vec u=\alpha\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat{j}+\gamma\hat{k}$, $\vec v=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat{i}+\beta\hat{j}+\delta\hat{k}$, $\vec w=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\hat{i}+\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\hat{j}+\mu\hat{k}$. Match each entry in List-I to the correct entry in List-II and choose the correct option.
List-I: (P) The value of $\gamma^2+\delta^2$ is; (Q) If $x\vec u+y\vec v+z\vec w=\hat{j}$ for some real numbers $x,y$ and $z$, then the value of $x$ is; (R) The value of $\left|\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)\right|$ is; (S) The value of $\left|\vec u\times(\vec v\times\vec w)\right|$ is.
List-II: (1) $0$; (2) $1$; (3) $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$; (4) $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$; (5) $\frac56$.
questions.key_idea: $MM^T=I$ makes the rows and the columns orthonormal, so $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ form an orthonormal triad.
solution: $MM^T=I$ means $M$ is orthogonal: its rows are orthonormal, and then $M^TM=I$ too, so its columns $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are orthonormal.
Row 1 has unit length: $\alpha^2+\frac12+\frac12=1$, so $\alpha=0$.
Row 1 $\cdot$ Row 2 $=0$: $\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt3}+\frac{\beta}{\sqrt2}-\frac{1}{\sqrt6}=0$, which with $\alpha=0$ gives $\beta=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$.
(P) Column 3 has unit length: $\frac12+\frac13+\mu^2=1$, so $\mu^2=\frac16$. Row 3 has unit length: $\gamma^2+\delta^2+\mu^2=1$, so $\gamma^2+\delta^2=\frac56$. (P) $\to$ (5).
Row 1 $\cdot$ Row 3 $=0$: $\alpha\gamma+\frac{\delta}{\sqrt2}-\frac{\mu}{\sqrt2}=0$, so $\delta=\mu$ (consistent with $\mu^2=\frac16$).
(Q) Since $\vec u\cdot\vec u=1$, $\vec u\cdot\vec v=0$, $\vec u\cdot\vec w=0$: dot $x\vec u+y\vec v+z\vec w=\hat{j}$ with $\vec u$ to get $x=\vec u\cdot\hat{j}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$. (Q) $\to$ (4).
(R) $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are three mutually perpendicular unit vectors, so the volume of the parallelepiped is $\left|\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)\right|=1$. (R) $\to$ (2).
(S) $\vec v\times\vec w=\pm\vec u$, so $\vec u\times(\vec v\times\vec w)=\pm\,\vec u\times\vec u=\vec 0$ and $\left|\vec u\times(\vec v\times\vec w)\right|=0$. (S) $\to$ (1).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use matrix facts directly: $M^{-1}=M^T$, $\det M=\pm1$, and $M(x,y,z)^T=\hat{j}$ gives $(x,y,z)^T$ as the second row of $M$.
solution: Rows and columns of $M$ are orthonormal; $M^{-1}=M^T$ and $\det M=\pm1$ (since $(\det M)^2=\det(MM^T)=1$).

(P) Column 3 is $\vec w=\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\mu\right)$ with unit length: $\mu^2=1-\frac12-\frac13=\frac16$. Row 3 $=(\gamma,\delta,\mu)$ also has unit length, so $\gamma^2+\delta^2=1-\frac16=\frac56$. (P) $\to$ (5). No need to find $\alpha,\beta$.

(Q) $x\vec u+y\vec v+z\vec w=M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}$ (columns $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$). So $M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=M^{T}\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, the second row of $M$ as a column.
Row 2 of $M$ is $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3},\beta,\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$, so $x=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$. (Q) $\to$ (4).
(R) $\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)=\det M$, so its absolute value is $1$. (R) $\to$ (2).
(S) $\vec u\times(\vec v\times\vec w)=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec w(\vec u\cdot\vec v)=\vec 0$ since $\vec u\perp\vec v$ and $\vec u\perp\vec w$. (S) $\to$ (1).

useful_results: For a square matrix, $MM^T=I\iff M^TM=I\iff$ rows orthonormal $\iff$ columns orthonormal; then $M^{-1}=M^T$ and $\det M=\pm1$.
Squared entries of any row or any column of an orthogonal matrix sum to $1$; this fixes unknowns from partial data (row 1: $\alpha^2+\frac12+\frac12=1\Rightarrow\alpha=0$).

If $\vec u,\vec v,\vec w$ are orthonormal then $\vec u\cdot(\vec v\times\vec w)=\det[\vec u\,\vec v\,\vec w]=\pm1$, $\vec v\times\vec w=\pm\vec u$, and the coordinates of any $\vec r$ in this basis are $x=\vec r\cdot\vec u$, $y=\vec r\cdot\vec v$, $z=\vec r\cdot\vec w$.
Vector triple product $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)=(\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$ lies in the plane of $\vec b,\vec c$; if $\vec a$ is perpendicular to both it vanishes.
